GEN.t: Where everything starts: creation, the fall, and God's promise to Abraham.
b: Genesis divides cleanly in two. Chapters 1–11 deal with the whole human race — creation, the fall, the flood, Babel — and answer why a good world contains so much that is wrong. Chapters 12–50 narrow to one family, beginning with God's promise to Abraham of a people, a land and a blessing that will reach every nation. Everything the rest of the Bible does is that promise working itself out.

Traditionally ascribed to Moses. Read it for the shape of the story rather than for isolated lessons: the first three chapters set up a problem that the last three chapters of Revelation resolve, and the correspondence is deliberate.

EXO.t: Rescue from slavery, the law at Sinai, and God moving in.
b: The central act of the Old Testament. God hears, remembers his covenant, and brings Israel out of Egypt by power. Then at Sinai he gives them a law — not as a means of earning rescue, which has already happened, but as the shape of life for a people already redeemed. The order matters and is easy to get backwards.
The last third, often skipped, concerns the tabernacle in exhausting detail. The payoff is the final verse: God comes to live in the middle of the camp. That is the point of the whole book.

LEV.t: How a holy God can live among an unholy people.
b: Hard going, and worth the effort once you know what it is for. Leviticus answers the question Exodus leaves open: if God now dwells in the camp, how does anyone survive the proximity? The answer involves sacrifice, priesthood and a sharp distinction between clean and unclean.
Read with Hebrews in the other hand. Almost every category here is picked up there and applied to Christ, who is presented as both the final sacrifice and the permanent priest.

NUM.t: Forty years of wandering, and why.
b: Israel arrives at the edge of the promised land within two years and refuses to enter. The rest of the book is the cost of that refusal. It is a sustained study in unbelief among people who had personally watched the sea part.
The generation that leaves Egypt is not the generation that enters. That is the warning Hebrews 3–4 draws from it.

DEU.t: Moses' last sermons, on the edge of the land.
b: A covenant document in the form of farewell speeches. Moses restates the law for a new generation who did not see Egypt, and the tone throughout is urgent: remember, do not forget, teach your children. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy more than any other book.
The heart of it is chapter 6 — love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul and strength — which Jesus identifies as the greatest commandment.

Conquest and division of territory under Joshua. The violence of these chapters is a genuine difficulty and should not be smoothed over; the text presents it as judgment on entrenched Canaanite practice, delayed for centuries, and it is bounded to this specific moment rather than offered as a pattern.
Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute, ends up in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The book is less ethnically tidy than it first appears.

JDG.t: The cycle that will not break.
b: Israel abandons God, is oppressed, cries out, is rescued by a judge, and then does it again. Six times. The judges themselves get steadily worse — by Samson the deliverer is barely distinguishable from the problem.
The refrain is that everyone did what was right in their own eyes. The book is an argument for why a king is needed, and a warning about what people are like without one.

RUT.t: Ordinary faithfulness in a brutal period.
b: Set during the judges, and deliberately so — a quiet story of loyalty set against a backdrop of chaos. A Moabite widow, an act of covenant kindness, and a redeemer who buys back what was lost.
It ends as a genealogy: Ruth is David's great-grandmother. God's purposes run through unremarkable decency as much as through great events.

1SA.t: Samuel, Saul, and the rise of David.
b: Israel demands a king like the other nations and gets exactly what it asked for. Saul looks the part and is hollow; David is overlooked and is not. The book's most repeated theme is that God does not see as people see.
The relationship between Saul and David is one of the most psychologically acute portraits in ancient literature.

The covenant of chapter 7 — God's promise that a descendant of David will reign for ever — is one of the load-bearing promises of Scripture, and the New Testament returns to it constantly. Chapter 11 is the counterweight: adultery, murder and a cover-up by the man after God's own heart.
Nothing is sanitised. The consequences run through the rest of the book and the rest of his family.

1KI.t: Solomon's glory, and the kingdom splitting.
b: Temple built, wisdom proverbial, wealth extraordinary — and then idolatry through marriage alliances, and a kingdom divided in a generation. From chapter 12 there are two nations, and the narrative alternates between them.
Elijah arrives in chapter 17 and the prophetic confrontation with state-sponsored idolatry begins.
Both kingdoms run down. The north falls to Assyria in 722 BC; the south survives longer under a few good kings but falls to Babylon, with Jerusalem and the temple destroyed around 586 BC.
The book ends with a small note of hope: the exiled king of Judah is released from prison and eats at the Babylonian king's table. The line is not extinguished.

1CH.t: The same history, retold for the returned exiles.
b: Chronicles covers much of Samuel and Kings again, but written after the exile for people rebuilding. The genealogies that open it establish continuity for a community that felt cut off from its past.
The emphasis falls on the temple, worship, and the Davidic line — the things that gave a diminished community its identity.
Solomon's temple, the kings of Judah, and the repeated cycle of reform and relapse. It ends with Cyrus's decree permitting the exiles to return, which is where Ezra picks up.
The return under Cyrus and the rebuilding of the temple against local opposition. Ezra himself arrives later, as a scribe committed to teaching the law to a community that had largely lost it.
Nehemiah leaves a comfortable post in the Persian court to rebuild Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days under sustained harassment. A practical book about leadership, opposition and organised work.
The reading of the law in chapter 8, and the weeping that follows, is the emotional centre.

EST.t: God's name never appears, and his hand is everywhere.
b: A Jewish woman becomes queen of Persia and prevents a genocide. God is not mentioned once in the Hebrew text, which is almost certainly deliberate: this is a book about providence working through coincidence, timing and human courage rather than through miracle.

The oldest sustained treatment of the question in Scripture. Job's friends offer the standard answer — suffering is punishment, so repent — and the book declares them wrong. Job demands an explanation and never receives one.

What he receives instead is God himself, in four chapters of questions about creation. The resolution is relational rather than informational, which is either deeply unsatisfying or exactly right depending on where you are when you read it.

A hundred and fifty prayers and songs, collected into five books, covering the entire emotional range. Roughly a third are laments — complaints, protests and demands — which is more than any other kind. God put a book of complaints inside his own book.
Jesus prayed these, quoted them constantly, and died with one on his lips. If you do not know what to pray, start here rather than trying to invent something.

Not promises but observations about how life generally works: about money, speech, work, sex, anger and friendship. Read as guarantees they will disappoint; read as the grain of the universe they are extremely useful.
Thirty-one chapters, which makes one a day for a month a natural habit.

Everything is vapour — fleeting, hard to grasp. The Preacher tries pleasure, work, wisdom and wealth and finds each insufficient. It is the most unsparing book in the Bible about the limits of life under the sun, and it has kept more honest doubters inside the faith than most apologetics.

Read for centuries as an allegory of Christ and the church, and more recently as what it plainly is: a celebration of desire and marriage within God's good creation. The two readings need not exclude each other, but the plain sense should not be explained away.

ISA.t: The biggest of the prophets, and the most quoted.
b: Judgment on Judah and the nations, then some of the clearest promises in the Old Testament of a coming king and a suffering Servant. Chapters 40–55 address the exile directly and contain the four Servant Songs, of which Isaiah 53 is the fourth.
The New Testament quotes Isaiah more than any book except Psalms.

JER.t: Forty years of saying what nobody wanted to hear.
b: Jeremiah warns Judah for decades, is beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern for it, and watches Jerusalem fall anyway. The most personally exposed of the prophets — his complaints to God are preserved alongside his preaching.
Chapter 31 contains the promise of a new covenant written on hearts, which Jesus takes up at the Last Supper.

Five poems over the ruin of Jerusalem, four of them acrostics. The formality is not coldness; it is grief given a container so it can be borne. At the exact centre sit the verses about mercies new every morning — hope, surrounded on both sides by devastation.
Strange, vivid and uncompromising. Ezekiel prophesies to the exiles in Babylon, with dramatised sign-acts and extended visions. The valley of dry bones in chapter 37 is the best known.
Chapter 34 — God against Israel's shepherds, promising to shepherd the flock himself — stands directly behind Jesus' shepherd language.
Six chapters of narrative — the furnace, the lions, the writing on the wall — followed by six of apocalyptic vision. Written partly in Aramaic.
Chapter 7's 'one like a son of man' who receives everlasting dominion is the passage Jesus repeatedly applies to himself, including at his trial.

God tells Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, so that his own life becomes the message. Israel's idolatry is presented as adultery, and God's response as the grief of a betrayed husband who will not let go.
A locust plague becomes the lens for a warning about judgment and a promise of restoration. Peter quotes chapter 2 at Pentecost to explain what has just happened.

Amos was a shepherd and fig-farmer, not a professional prophet, and he indicts a prosperous Israel for trampling the poor while maintaining an active religious life. The sharpest social-justice material in the prophets.
The shortest book in the Old Testament. Judgment on Edom for standing by — and gloating — while Jerusalem fell.
Jonah runs not because the task is dangerous but because he suspects God will forgive Nineveh, and he is right. A short book with an unresolved ending and a sharp point about who God's mercy is for.
Judgment and hope in alternation, from a contemporary of Isaiah. Chapter 5 names Bethlehem; chapter 6 asks what God requires and answers: act justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.
The city spared in Jonah has not stayed repentant. Nahum announces its fall. Read alongside Jonah, the two books together say something careful about patience and its limits.

Habakkuk objects that God is ignoring evil, and then objects harder when told the remedy is Babylon. The exchange is preserved in full. It ends in one of the most defiant statements of trust in Scripture — though the crops fail and the stalls stand empty, yet I will rejoice.
The line 'the righteous will live by faith' comes from here, and Paul builds on it twice.

ZEP.t: The day of the LORD, again.
b: Judgment on Judah and the nations, followed by a promise of a humble remnant. Chapter 3 ends with God rejoicing over his people with singing.
Two chapters, urging returned exiles who have panelled their own houses while God's house lies in ruins. Brief and pointed about misplaced priorities.

Eight night visions, then oracles pointing forward. Densely messianic — the king coming humble on a donkey, the shepherd struck, the thirty pieces of silver, the one they pierced. The Gospels draw on it heavily in the passion narratives.

MAL.t: The last word before four hundred years of silence.
b: A dispute-format book: God makes a charge, the people answer back, God responds. Half-hearted worship, broken marriages and withheld offerings. It ends looking forward to a messenger who will prepare the way — which is where Mark begins.

MAT.t: The Jewish Gospel: Jesus as the promised king.
b: Matthew writes for readers who know the Old Testament, and his constant refrain is that this happened to fulfil what was spoken. He opens with a genealogy tying Jesus to Abraham and David, and organises his teaching material into five blocks, of which the Sermon on the Mount is the first.
The ending — all authority, go and make disciples — is the commission on which the rest of church history hangs.

LUK.t: The historian's Gospel, and the one for outsiders.
b: Luke states his method in the opening paragraph: he investigated carefully and wrote an orderly account. A doctor and a Gentile, writing for a Gentile, he gives more attention than anyone else to women, the poor, Samaritans and the socially disregarded.
The parables unique to Luke — the good Samaritan, the prodigal son — are among the best known things Jesus ever said.

JHN.t: The fourth Gospel: written so that you may believe.
b: Different in texture from the other three. Long discourses rather than short scenes, seven signs rather than many miracles, and seven 'I am' statements that pick up the divine name from Exodus. John states his purpose explicitly near the end: these are written so that you may believe.
It is the deepest of the Gospels and, oddly, often the first recommended — simple language, profound content.

ACT.t: How a Jewish sect became a worldwide church in thirty years.
b: Luke's second volume. The Spirit comes at Pentecost and the message moves from Jerusalem outward, breaking through every barrier the early church assumed was fixed — Samaritans, an Ethiopian official, a Roman centurion, and finally Gentiles in large numbers.
It ends without resolution, with Paul under house arrest in Rome still preaching. The story is presented as unfinished on purpose.

ROM.t: The fullest explanation of the gospel anywhere.
b: Paul writes to a church he has not founded, setting out his message systematically: all humanity under sin, righteousness from God through faith in Christ, the place of Israel, and the shape of a transformed life. It has triggered more than one reformation.
Dense, and worth going slowly. Chapters 1–8 are the argument; 9–11 handle Israel; 12 onward is application.

1CO.t: A troubled church, addressed point by point.
b: Divisions, lawsuits, sexual immorality, disputes over food, chaos at the Lord's Supper and confusion about gifts. Paul takes the issues in turn. The results include chapter 13 on love and chapter 15 on the resurrection, both written as corrections rather than as set pieces.

2CO.t: The most personal thing Paul wrote.
b: A defence of his ministry against opponents in Corinth, and in the course of it the clearest New Testament material on weakness, suffering and comfort. The thorn in the flesh, and the answer that grace is sufficient, comes near the end.

Paul's angriest letter. Teachers have arrived in Galatia requiring Gentile converts to keep the law, and Paul treats this not as a secondary disagreement but as a different religion. Justification by faith apart from works of the law is argued here at white heat.

EPH.t: What being a Christian actually means.
b: Three chapters of theology — chosen, redeemed, raised, brought near, made one — followed by three of application. Short, dense, and best taken a few verses at a time.
Chapter 2 verses 8 to 10 is as compact a statement of grace as the New Testament contains.

Warm and personal, written while Paul is in custody, and full of joy anyway. Chapter 2 contains an early hymn about Christ emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, which is among the highest Christology in the New Testament.

Written against teaching that added philosophical and ritual requirements to Christ. Paul's answer is to make the largest possible claims about him: the image of the invisible God, the one in whom all things hold together, in whom the fullness of deity dwells bodily.
Chapter 1 verses 15 to 20 is the passage most often argued over with Jehovah's Witnesses, and repays careful reading.
One of Paul's earliest letters. Encouragement for a young church under pressure, and instruction about Christians who have died before Christ's return — which was evidently causing distress.
Some in Thessalonica had concluded the day of the Lord had already come and had stopped working. Paul corrects the theology and then, bluntly, the behaviour.
Practical instruction to a younger leader about teaching, elders, deacons, money and false doctrine. The first of the three Pastoral Letters.
Written expecting execution. Personal, urgent, and focused on handing on the deposit of faith intact. The charge to preach the word, in season and out, comes from here.

TIT.t: Sound doctrine and good works together.
b: Short instruction for church order in Crete, with a strong insistence that what is believed and how people live cannot be separated.

PHM.t: A runaway slave, returned as a brother.
b: The shortest of Paul's letters, and a masterclass in persuasion. Paul does not command Philemon to free Onesimus; he makes it almost impossible for him not to, and plants the principle that dismantled the institution over time.

Written to Jewish Christians tempted to go back, and arguing on their own ground: Christ is greater than angels, than Moses, than the priesthood, than the sacrificial system. Leviticus makes far more sense after reading it.
Chapter 10 verses 23 to 25 — hold fast, consider one another, do not neglect meeting together — is the passage the Community of Brothers takes its name and its shape from.

Blunt, practical, and closer to Proverbs than to Paul in style. Speech, money, favouritism, patience. The apparent conflict with Paul on faith and works dissolves once you notice they are answering different questions.
Written to scattered believers facing hostility, urging endurance and conduct that gives the accusations nothing to hold on to. Realistic about suffering without ever presenting it as meaningless.

2PE.t: Watch for teachers who make things up.
b: A warning against false teaching and against scoffers who use the delay of Christ's return as an argument. The delay, Peter says, is patience, not absence.

Written so that believers may know they have eternal life. Three recurring tests — belief about Jesus, obedience, and love for other Christians. Short, circular in structure, and unusually comforting for the genuinely anxious.
A single chapter, warning against extending support to travelling teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh.

3JN.t: A church power struggle in miniature.
b: Commendation of one man's hospitality, and complaint about another who likes being first and excludes those he dislikes.
A short, fierce warning about people who have slipped in and turned grace into a licence. Notable for quoting sources outside the Old Testament canon, which has occupied scholars ever since.

Apocalyptic literature, written to seven real churches under pressure, using a symbolic vocabulary its first readers understood far better than we do. Read it for its argument rather than as a coded timetable: God wins, the Lamb who was slain is on the throne, and faithfulness under pressure is worth it.
The last two chapters answer the first two of Genesis — a garden becomes a city, and God lives with his people face to face.

MRK.t: The shortest and fastest Gospel. Almost certainly the first written, and the one that puts the question of who Jesus is in front of you within a page.
b: Who wrote it. The Gospel itself is anonymous, but the early tradition is unusually consistent. Papias, writing around AD 130 and quoted later by Eusebius, records that Mark acted as Peter’s interpreter and wrote down accurately what Peter preached, though not in order. That fits the man the New Testament calls John Mark — the one whose mother hosted the church in Jerusalem, who abandoned Paul on the first missionary journey, and whom Paul later asked for by name as useful to him. It is not the reputation a later writer would invent for an author.

When and for whom. Most place it in the 60s, around the time of Peter’s death in Rome and the persecution under Nero. The audience is clearly not Jewish: Mark stops to explain Jewish handwashing customs, translates every Aramaic phrase he quotes, and uses Latin loanwords where a Greek term existed. He is writing for Gentile believers who may soon face what Peter faced, which explains why a Gospel this short spends so much of itself on suffering.

How it is built. The whole thing turns on one question, asked at the exact midpoint: “But who do you say that I am?” Everything before chapter 8 builds the case through authority — over sickness, demons, the sea, the law, death itself. Everything after it redefines what that authority means, through three predictions of the cross, each followed by the disciples misunderstanding and Jesus teaching them what following actually costs.

The pace. Mark uses the word “immediately” around forty times. Sentences run into each other. There is very little teaching material compared with Matthew or Luke, and a great deal of movement. The effect is deliberate: you are pulled toward Jerusalem almost faster than you can think, which is roughly how it must have felt.

The secret. Jesus repeatedly silences demons and tells the healed to say nothing. A century ago William Wrede argued this was invented by the early church to explain why nobody recognised Jesus as Messiah during his lifetime. The better explanation is simpler and is Mark’s own: the title “Messiah” carried expectations of a military deliverer, and it cannot be safely used until the cross has redefined it. Jesus accepts the title openly only once he is on trial and has nothing left to lose by it.

The frame. Mark opens by calling Jesus the Son of God, and the next human being to say it is a Roman execution officer standing in front of a corpse. Between those two points, no human character in the Gospel gets it right. That is the argument of the book: you do not understand who Jesus is until you have looked at the cross.

1.h: The first line is the thesis
1.t: Mark does not open with a genealogy or a nativity but with a claim. “Beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis: something is starting here on that scale. “Gospel” was not yet a religious word — in the Roman world it announced an imperial victory or the birth of an emperor. To attach it to an executed Galilean is a political provocation as much as a theological one. Note the footnote: some early manuscripts lack “the Son of God”, though the phrase reappears at the centre and the climax of the book regardless.

1.h: All three persons at the Jordan
1.t: The Son is baptised, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The Trinity is not a doctrine developed centuries later and read backwards into the text; it is simply what is happening in this scene. The Father’s words splice Psalm 2:7, spoken to the messianic king, with Isaiah 42:1, spoken to the suffering Servant. Both identities are assigned before Jesus has done anything, and the tension between them drives the rest of the Gospel.

Mark gives the temptation two verses where Matthew and Luke give forty. The verb is violent — the Spirit throws him out into the wilderness. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness and failed; Jesus spends forty days and does not. The wild animals are Mark’s detail alone, and may hint at Eden restored.

Nothing is said about why they follow. Mark is not interested in their psychology but in his authority: he speaks, and men leave their livelihood mid-shift. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired men, which tells you this was a business of some size. Following costs something real from the first sentence.

The crowd’s reaction is that he teaches with authority, “not as the scribes”. A scribe’s authority was derivative — he cited those before him. Jesus cites nobody. The demon, notably, is the first character in the Gospel to identify him correctly, and is immediately silenced. Throughout Mark the supernatural realm knows exactly who he is while the human characters do not.

Under the law, touching a leper made you unclean. Jesus touches him and the man is cleansed instead. The direction of contagion reverses. This is a small picture of the whole gospel: holiness that goes out and absorbs rather than holiness that withdraws and protects itself.

2.t: The scribes’ reasoning is impeccable: only God forgives sins, therefore this is blasphemy. Their logic is right and their conclusion is wrong, and the only way out is the one they will not take. Jesus does not soften the claim; he proves it with something visible. “Son of Man” here is not a modest self-description — it is drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where a human figure approaches the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion.

Levi collected tax for Rome from his own people, which made him a collaborator as well as a thief. Table fellowship in this culture signalled acceptance, which is precisely why the objection is raised. Jesus’ reply is not that these people are fine as they are — he calls them sick and himself the doctor. Both halves of that matter.

2.h: Not a patch on the old
2.t: The new wine imagery is often softened into a general point about change. Its actual force is sharper: what Jesus brings cannot be contained inside the existing structures of Second Temple religion. Something is being replaced, not renovated.

3.h: The alliance that should not exist
3.t: Pharisees were religious separatists; Herodians were political collaborators with Rome. They agreed on almost nothing except, now, this. Mark places the decision to kill Jesus in chapter three of sixteen — the outcome is fixed before a third of the book has passed, and everything after moves toward it.

The number is the point. Twelve tribes, twelve apostles: Jesus is constituting a renewed Israel around himself. Judas is named in the list from the beginning, with his end already attached, which Mark does without comment.

This passage has caused more unnecessary fear than almost any other. What Jesus condemns is the settled, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit’s work to Satan — looking at undeniable good and calling it evil in order to avoid its implications. It is a hardened position, not a moment of doubt or a blasphemous thought that intruded. The pastoral point follows logically: anyone anxious about having committed it has demonstrated by that anxiety that they have not. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

Mark sandwiches the Beelzebul controversy inside the story of Jesus’ family coming to seize him because they think he is out of his mind. The structure is intentional. Both his relatives and the religious authorities conclude something is wrong with him; the difference is only in what they blame.

4.t: The parable is not primarily about identifying which soil you are. It is an explanation of why the ministry is producing such mixed results, and a promise that despite the waste the harvest will be absurdly large. Thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were extraordinary yields in first-century Palestine, where sevenfold was a good year.

4.h: The hardest verses in the chapter
4.t: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 to explain that parables both reveal and conceal. This sits uncomfortably with modern assumptions, and it should. The point is that hearing is not a neutral capacity everyone possesses and some choose to use; genuine understanding is given. Those already resisting find that the parables harden the resistance. This is why the disciples’ access to explanation is a gift rather than a reward — they understand no better than anyone else, as the next four chapters repeatedly show. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something God does and nobody else — Psalm 107:29 is the closest parallel and the disciples would have known it. Their terror after the calm is greater than their terror during the storm, and rightly so. The question they ask is Mark’s question, and he will not answer it plainly until chapter 8.

5.t: A Roman legion was roughly six thousand men, and the name is unlikely to be accidental in a Gospel written for readers under Roman power. The setting is Gentile territory — hence the pigs — and the healed man becomes the first person commissioned to tell rather than to keep silent. Outside Israel, the misunderstanding that the secret protects against does not apply.

Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus’s story, and the two are linked by the number twelve — she has bled for twelve years, the girl is twelve years old. Both are ritually unclean situations; both are reversed by touch. Jairus has to stand and wait while his daughter dies, which is Mark’s honest acknowledgement that delay is part of the experience even when the outcome is good.
Mark preserves the actual words — talitha koum — and then translates them. He does this several times. It is the kind of detail that survives when a story comes from someone who was in the room.

6.t: Mark says plainly that Jesus could do no miracle there beyond a few healings, and that he marvelled at their unbelief. This is not a statement about a shortage of divine power; it is a statement about the nature of what he came to do. Miracles in Mark are never displays for their own sake — they meet faith, and where there is none they have nothing to meet.

The execution of John is the single passage in Mark where Jesus does not appear, and it is told in unusual detail. Its placement, between the sending of the Twelve and their return, is a warning shot: this is what happens to those who speak for God to people in power. Mark’s first readers, under Nero, would not have missed it.

“Sheep without a shepherd” is a quotation, not a sentiment — it comes from Numbers 27:17 and is picked up in Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s leaders and promises to shepherd the flock himself. Sitting them down on green grass points at Psalm 23. Mark is telling you who is doing the feeding.

6.h: He meant to pass by them
6.t: An odd detail until you notice where it comes from. In Exodus 33 and 1 Kings 19, God “passes by” Moses and Elijah — it is the technical language of a divine appearance. Combined with the words rendered “It is I”, which in Greek are simply “I am”, this is a theophany on the water. Mark closes by noting the disciples’ hearts were hardened, using the same word he applies to the Pharisees.

7.t: The specific abuse is declaring property dedicated to the temple so that it becomes unavailable to support ageing parents, while the declarer retains its use. Jesus’ charge is not that tradition is worthless but that this tradition is being used to cancel a commandment. The principle generalises uncomfortably well.

The clause declaring all foods clean is Mark’s editorial note, not part of Jesus’ speech. It is a remarkable thing for a first-century Jewish writer to say, and it indicates how far the implications had been worked out by the time he wrote. The food laws that separated Israel from the nations are over.

7.h: The only person who wins an argument
7.t: Jesus’ words to the Syrophoenician woman are deliberately hard, and attempts to soften them usually make the passage worse. She does not dispute the priority he states — she accepts it and presses for the overflow. She is the only character in the Gospels who takes Jesus’ own image and turns it, and he commends her for exactly that. Immediately afterwards he feeds a Gentile crowd.

8.t: Two feedings have happened and the disciples worry about bread. Jesus’ questions here — do you have eyes and fail to see, ears and fail to hear — apply to the disciples the same language chapter 4 applied to outsiders. The gap between them and the crowd is smaller than they think.

The only miracle in the Gospels that takes two attempts, and it is placed here deliberately. The man first sees people looking like walking trees, then sees clearly. In the very next scene Peter identifies Jesus correctly and then immediately misunderstands what it means. The healing is a deliberate commentary on the confession that follows.

Caesarea Philippi was a centre of pagan worship, which makes it a pointed place to ask the question. Peter’s answer is right, and Jesus orders silence. This is the midpoint of the book; from here the geography turns toward Jerusalem and the subject turns to the cross.

Peter is rebuked in the strongest terms in the Gospel, moments after being right. The rebuke is not for doubting that Jesus is Messiah but for assuming he knows what a Messiah does. Note the word “must” in the prediction — the cross is not a tragic accident that befalls the plan; it is the plan.

9.t: Moses and Elijah represent the law and the prophets; their presence and then their disappearance, leaving Jesus alone, is the point of the scene. The Father’s command echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. Peter’s instinct to build shelters is an attempt to make a permanent arrangement of a moment that was never meant to be one.

9.h: The most honest prayer in the Bible
9.t: “I believe; help my unbelief” is a contradiction, and it is answered anyway. It is worth noticing what Jesus does not do: he does not tell the man to come back when he is more certain. Faith that is mixed with doubt is still faith, and it is still enough. Most Christians will pray this sentence at some point, and they are in good company.

The second passion prediction is followed immediately by the disciples debating which of them is greatest. Mark reports this without editorial comment, which is its own comment. Jesus’ answer places a child — a person of no status whatever in that society — at the centre of the room.

10.t: Asked to take a side in a rabbinic dispute about grounds for divorce, Jesus goes past the Mosaic concession to Genesis. The permission existed, he says, because of hardness of heart — a regulation of failure rather than a statement of intent. He treats the creation account as normative and as historical, which is worth noting on its own.

10.h: Jesus looked at him and loved him
10.t: Mark alone records the look and the love, which changes the tone of everything that follows. The demand is not a general requirement laid on all disciples but a diagnosis of this man’s particular idol, aimed precisely. The disciples’ astonishment reflects an assumption that wealth signalled God’s favour. Jesus’ answer — that it is impossible for anyone, and possible only with God — is as clear a statement of salvation by grace as the Gospels contain.

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. “Ransom” is a marketplace and slave-market word: a price paid to secure release. “For many” echoes Isaiah 53:11–12 and the Servant who bears the sins of many. Every major strand of the New Testament’s understanding of the cross is already present in this one sentence, spoken by Jesus about himself.

Bartimaeus is the only person healed in Mark whose name is recorded. He addresses Jesus as Son of David — a messianic title — and is not silenced, because Jerusalem is now in view. Mark ends the account by saying he followed Jesus on the road, and the road leads directly to the cross. He is the model disciple, and he is a blind beggar.

11.t: The arrangements are too specific to be spontaneous. Jesus is staging Zechariah 9:9 — a king coming humble and riding on a donkey, the animal of peace rather than the warhorse. The crowd’s shout comes from Psalm 118. They are expecting a different kind of king from the one they have.

11.h: The fig tree and the temple
11.t: Mark splits the fig tree around the temple cleansing, which is the clearest example of his sandwiching technique. The tree is in leaf but bears nothing; the temple is in operation but produces nothing. One interprets the other. The quotation about a house of prayer for all nations comes from Isaiah 56:7, and the trading was taking place in the only court Gentiles were permitted to enter.

Jesus' promises about prayer are real and bold, but they sit inside the rest of Scripture, where Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and was not spared, and Paul's thorn was not removed. The historic Christian understanding is that God always hears and always answers in love, sometimes by giving what we ask, sometimes by giving something better, and sometimes by giving himself in the waiting. Unanswered prayer is not usually evidence of weak faith; it is one of the ordinary experiences of every believer in Scripture. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

12.t: The vineyard is Isaiah 5, and the audience recognised it immediately — Mark tells us they knew the parable was about them. The escalation from servants to the beloved son is the whole history of Israel’s prophets, and Jesus places himself at the end of it in a category of his own.

The trap is real: say yes and lose the crowd, say no and face Rome. Jesus’ answer is not a tidy separation of religion and politics. The coin bears Caesar’s image so return it to him — and you bear God’s image, so the question of what is owed to God answers itself and is not a small one.

Usually read as a lesson in generosity, and it is. But notice its placement, directly after Jesus condemns scribes who devour widows’ houses and immediately before he predicts the temple’s destruction. The woman gives everything to an institution that is about to fall and that has been exploiting people like her. The admiration and the lament are held together.

13.t: Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world and some of its foundation stones weighed over fifty tonnes. The prediction was literally fulfilled in AD 70, within the lifetime of many who heard it.

The discourse moves between the fall of Jerusalem and the final return, and interpreters divide over where the line falls. The most defensible reading takes the detailed warnings about Judea as concerning AD 70, and the cosmic language from verse 24 as concerning the end. Whatever the division, the repeated instruction is not to calculate but to stay awake — and Jesus states plainly that the day is not known even to the Son. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

14.h: She has done what she could
14.t: The perfume was worth close to a year’s wages. The objection about the poor is reasonable, and Jesus does not dismiss it so much as subordinate it to the moment. Sandwiched between Judas’s betrayal arrangements on either side, the contrast is stark: one person pours out everything, another sells him for silver.

“This is my body” is said while his body is visibly present, which should govern how literally the words are taken. The covenant language comes from Exodus 24 and Jeremiah 31. Christians have divided for centuries over what happens at the table; what is not in dispute is that his death is being interpreted, by him, in advance, as a sacrifice that establishes a covenant.

Mark preserves the Aramaic word for Father, the ordinary family word. The prayer asks for the cup to pass and then submits, and both halves are recorded. This is the clearest window in the Gospels into the genuine humanity of Jesus — not a performance of distress but distress. That he asks and is not spared says something important about what unanswered prayer can mean.

Asked directly whether he is the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One, Jesus answers with two words that in Greek are simply “I am”, and then combines Daniel 7 with Psalm 110. He claims divine identity, enthronement and the role of coming judge in one sentence. The high priest’s reaction shows the claim was understood exactly as intended.

If this Gospel carries Peter’s testimony, then the most humiliating account of Peter in the New Testament comes from Peter. Mark records no rehabilitation scene; the only forward-looking word is the message at the tomb that names Peter specifically.

15.t: Jesus quotes the opening line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic. Two things are true at once and both matter. He is genuinely bearing abandonment, and he is reaching for Scripture to say so — and Psalm 22, which begins in that darkness, ends in vindication and worldwide worship. The quotation is not despair with no floor under it.
The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from everything else and enforced the distance between God and people. Mark specifies the direction of the tear. This is not something achieved from below.

Mark’s whole argument lands here. The first human being in the Gospel to confess Jesus as Son of God is a Roman officer who has just supervised his execution, and what convinces him is not a miracle but the manner of the death. This closes the frame opened in 1:1 — and the fact that it is a Gentile who sees it first would not have been lost on Mark’s readers in Rome.

16.h: An ending that does not feel like one
16.t: The women are told that he is risen and that the disciples — and Peter by name — will see him. Then they flee and say nothing, and the Greek text ends on a conjunction, mid-breath. Many readers have found this unsatisfying; it may be exactly the point. The one group in the Gospel who obey and speak are the readers, and Mark has left the last move to them.

Most modern Bibles mark this passage off, and the BSB is no exception. The two earliest and most reliable complete manuscripts of Mark end at verse 8, as do several early translations and patristic witnesses; the longer ending uses vocabulary and style found nowhere else in Mark. Some manuscripts carry a shorter alternative ending instead. None of this is hidden or recent — translators flag it precisely because the evidence is public, and no Christian doctrine depends on these verses. It is a good example of textual criticism working as it should.

1.h: The question they ask, and the one he answers
1.t: They want to know about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel. Jesus does not correct the hope, he reframes its scope: not a date to be calculated but a mission to be carried out, and verse 8 is the table of contents for the whole book — Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth.

The ascension is not Jesus disappearing but Jesus being enthroned. The promise that he will return in the same way makes the second coming bodily and visible, which rules out spiritualised readings of it.

1.h: Casting lots, for the last time
1.t: The replacement of Judas restores the Twelve to their symbolic completeness before Pentecost. Note that this is the final time in Scripture anyone seeks guidance by lot; after chapter 2 the Spirit is given, and the method never recurs.

2.t: Fifty days after Passover, at the feast celebrating the giving of the law at Sinai. Wind and fire are both Sinai imagery. What was written on stone is now written on people, exactly as Jeremiah 31 promised.
At Babel one language became many and the people scattered. Here many languages hear one message and people are gathered. Luke lists the nations deliberately.

Peter's argument is almost entirely Old Testament: Joel, Psalm 16, Psalm 110. He does not ask them to accept a new religion but to recognise that their own Scriptures have been fulfilled. The conclusion in verse 36 — God has made him both Lord and Christ — is the point everything builds to.

Peter ties baptism and forgiveness together in one sentence, which has been read in two ways: that baptism conveys forgiveness, or that it is the appointed sign of the repentance and faith through which forgiveness comes. The second is the Reformed and broadly evangelical reading, and the rest of Acts supports it — in chapter 10 the Spirit falls before anyone is baptised. However you read the order, the New Testament never imagines an unbaptised Christian. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
Four things: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer. Everything the church has since become complicated about is in that one verse in its simplest form.

3.h: Silver and gold I do not have
3.t: The healing happens at the temple gate, to a man who had been carried there daily for years. Note that Peter takes him by the hand — the same physical directness Jesus used.
Peter grants that they did not know what they were doing, which is startling given what they did. The offer of repentance is extended to the men who called for the crucifixion weeks earlier.

4.t: The exclusivity claim of the New Testament, stated plainly by a fisherman to the ruling council. It is worth noticing that this is said in a courtroom, under threat, rather than in a sermon to sympathetic hearers.
The council's assessment is accurate and their explanation is the key: they recognised that these men had been with Jesus. Competence is not what is being described.

5.t: The severity troubles people, and it should. The sin is not withholding — Peter says the property and the money were theirs — but lying to appear more generous than they were. It happens at the foundation of the church, and the effect is fear, which Luke reports without apology. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

5.h: Why did Ananias and Sapphira die
5.t: Their sin was not keeping money back — Peter says it was theirs — but lying to God to appear more generous than they were, at the very foundation of the church. Luke records the fear it produced without softening it. The episode is exceptional rather than a pattern: the New Testament does not expect such judgement to follow every sin, and later passages show great patience with serious failure. It stands as a warning that God is not mocked, especially where religion becomes performance. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

5.h: Lied to the Spirit, lied to God
5.t: Peter names the Holy Spirit as the one lied to, then in the next breath names God. The two statements are doing the same work, which is one of the clearest indications in Acts of the Spirit's full deity.

Sound counsel from a man who is not a believer, and Luke records it because history vindicated it. It is not, however, a reliable general principle: plenty of false movements have outlasted a generation.

6.t: A complaint about unequal treatment of Greek-speaking widows. Note the solution: the apostles do not take it on themselves but delegate, and all seven men chosen have Greek names — the complaining group is given the responsibility.

7.t: The longest speech in Acts, and it is a retelling of Israel's history with one thread pulled through it: God has always worked outside the land and outside the temple, and his people have always resisted those he sent.
Stephen sees Jesus standing — not seated — at God's right hand, and prays directly to him. His final words echo Jesus' own on the cross. Watching it is a man named Saul.

8.t: The scattering that was meant to destroy the church spreads it. Luke notes drily that those scattered preached wherever they went, and the gospel reaches Samaria as verse 1:8 said it would.

Reading Isaiah 53 and asking who the prophet means. Philip begins from that passage and tells him about Jesus, which is a model for how the Old Testament is to be preached. The man goes back to Africa with the message.

9.t: The question Jesus asks — why do you persecute me — identifies himself with the church he is not physically among. Paul's conversion is not a decision he arrives at but an intervention he is subjected to, which shapes everything he later writes about grace.
Nobody trusted Saul, understandably. Barnabas vouched for him, and the entire Gentile mission traces back through that one act of risk.

10.h: Cornelius, and the conversion of Peter
10.t: This chapter is usually called the conversion of Cornelius, but the man who changes most is Peter. The vision is repeated three times because he resists it twice.
The theological breakthrough of the book. Peter's summary of the gospel here is the shortest in Acts and worth memorising.

11.t: The first church where Gentiles are evangelised as a matter of course, and the place believers are first called Christians — probably as a nickname by outsiders. It becomes the base for everything that follows.

12.h: Praying for something and not believing it
12.t: The church prays for Peter's release, and when he turns up at the door they tell the servant girl she is out of her mind. Luke's sense of humour is real and this is the clearest example of it.

13.t: The Holy Spirit speaks in the first person — set apart for me — and claims both the calling and the men. Forces do not speak that way.
Paul's first recorded sermon already contains the doctrine of justification by faith, and states it as something the law of Moses could not accomplish.

14.t: The same crowd that tried to sacrifice to them drags Paul out for dead within days. Paul's speech to pagans here is entirely different from his synagogue preaching — he starts from creation rather than from Scripture.
Having just been stoned, Paul goes back to the cities he was driven from to strengthen the disciples, telling them hardship is the road in. He is not offering an easy gospel.

15.t: The most consequential meeting in church history. The question is whether Gentile converts must become Jews first, and the answer is no — salvation is by grace through faith for everybody on the same terms.

15.h: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
15.t: The council names the Spirit alongside themselves as party to the decision, which is not how anyone speaks about an impersonal influence.
Over John Mark, who had abandoned them earlier. Luke reports the sharp disagreement without resolving it. Mark later becomes useful to Paul and writes a Gospel.

16.t: The Spirit prevents them twice before the Macedonian vision. Guidance in Acts is as often a blocked route as a clear call.
Luke's description of Lydia's conversion puts the initiative squarely with God. She is already a worshipper, already listening — and still the opening is done to her.
Singing after a beating, an earthquake, and a jailer who was about to kill himself. The question he asks and the answer he gets are about as compressed as the gospel gets.

17.t: Commended for checking the Scriptures daily to see whether what Paul said was true — of an apostle. The public-domain Bible on this site takes its name from them.
Paul quotes pagan poets rather than Scripture, starts from an altar they built themselves, and still ends at repentance and resurrection. Contextualisation without dilution.

18.t: Paul evidently needed telling. He stays in Corinth eighteen months, which is the longest he has settled anywhere so far.

19.t: The Ephesian converts destroy magic scrolls worth fifty thousand drachmas — roughly fifty thousand days' wages. Repentance costs them something specific.
The silversmiths' objection is commercial and only afterwards religious. Luke lets Demetrius say so himself.

20.h: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders
20.t: The only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders. Note verse 28: the church of God, bought with his own blood — one of the strongest statements of Christ's deity in the book, and a disputed text worth knowing about.

20.h: A saying not in the Gospels
20.t: More blessed to give than to receive is attributed to Jesus but appears in none of the four Gospels. Evidence that more of his teaching circulated than was written down.

21.t: Agabus predicts Paul's imprisonment accurately; the believers conclude he should not go. Paul disagrees. The prediction is from the Spirit; the inference drawn from it is not.

22.t: Paul's testimony, adapted for a Jewish crowd in Aramaic. Luke gives the Damascus road three times in this book. The detail that ends the speech — sent to the Gentiles — is what ends the hearing.

23.t: Paul sets Pharisee against Sadducee on the resurrection. Shrewd, arguably too shrewd, and Luke neither praises nor criticises it.

24.t: Paul speaks about righteousness, self-control and the judgement to come, and Felix is frightened enough to send him away — then keeps him two years hoping for a bribe. The most honest picture in Scripture of a man who is interested but will not move.

25.t: A Roman citizen's right, and the mechanism by which Paul gets to Rome at imperial expense. God's purposes run through legal procedure here rather than around it.

26.t: Agrippa's reply is famously ambiguous in the Greek and may be sarcasm. Paul's answer — that he wishes everyone listening were as he is, except for the chains — is one of the warmest things he ever said.

27.t: An unusually detailed sea narrative, and one of the passages where Luke's eyewitness accuracy can be checked against what is known of ancient seafaring. It holds up.

28.t: Paul closes his ministry in Acts quoting the same passage Jesus used about hardened hearing, and attributes the speech to the Holy Spirit speaking through Isaiah — where Isaiah 6 says it was the Lord.
Two years under house arrest, preaching without hindrance, and then the book simply stops. No verdict, no execution, no resolution. The story is presented as still running.

1.t: Verses 3 to 14 are a single sentence in Greek, structured around three movements that each end in praise of God's glory — the Father choosing, the Son redeeming, the Spirit sealing. The Trinity structures the paragraph before any doctrine is stated.

1.h: Chosen before the foundation of the world
1.t: Election is stated plainly here and it is stated as a comfort rather than a puzzle: chosen in him, before creation, for adoption. Paul's tone is worship, not debate, and the doctrine is meant to produce the same in us.
Note what he prays for — not for circumstances to change, but that they would know what they already have. The power described in verse 19 is measured against the resurrection.

2.t: Paul's diagnosis is not that we were weakened but that we were dead, walking according to the age, the ruler of the air, and our own desires. A dead man contributes nothing to his own rescue, which is the point of the next verse.

The hinge of the letter and arguably of the New Testament. Salvation by grace through faith, not from ourselves, not by works, so that nobody can boast — followed immediately by verse 10, which puts works in their right place as the result rather than the cause.

The second half of the chapter applies the same grace to the Jew–Gentile division. The dividing wall is probably the literal barrier in the temple court beyond which Gentiles could not pass on pain of death.

3.t: A mystery in the New Testament is not something unknowable but something previously hidden and now disclosed. Here it is that Gentiles are fellow heirs — not admitted to the edges of Israel but made co-members of one body.
Paul prays for strength in the inner man, indwelling by Christ, and comprehension of a love that he immediately says surpasses knowledge. The doxology in verses 20–21 is the high point of the letter.

4.t: The turn from doctrine to life. The seven ones of verses 4 to 6 — one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God and Father — are the basis of unity rather than a target to achieve.
The gifted leaders are given to equip the saints for the work of ministry, not to do it for them. The whole body grows as each part works.

5.t: A sustained contrast between the old life and the new, ending in the Spirit-filled life marked by singing and thanksgiving. Note that being filled with the Spirit is a command, and its evidence here is corporate rather than ecstatic.

The passage begins with mutual submission in verse 21 before any instruction to wives. Paul's demand of husbands is not authority but Christlike self-sacrifice, measured by the cross. He then says the whole arrangement was always about Christ and the church. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

6.t: Every piece is drawn from Isaiah's description of God's own armour — the armour is his, lent to us. Note that the struggle is explicitly not against flesh and blood, and that prayer is where the passage ends rather than an extra item.

1.t: The confidence is in God's persistence, not ours. Paul writes this to a church he is fond of and cannot visit.
Paul genuinely cannot decide which he would prefer, and settles it on the basis of what is more useful to them. Written from custody, with execution a live possibility.

2.t: Probably an early hymn Paul is quoting. It describes Christ as existing in the form of God, not grasping at equality, emptying himself, obeying to the point of the cross, and then being exalted and given the name above every name.
Paul applies Isaiah 45:23 — an oath Jehovah swears by himself, that to him every knee will bow — directly to Jesus. That transfer is one of the strongest Christological moves in the New Testament.

2.h: Work out, because God works in
2.t: The two halves must be held together. Our effort is real and it is the evidence of God's prior working, not an alternative to it.

3.t: Paul lists his credentials — the best available — and then uses a deliberately coarse word for what he now considers them. The righteousness he wants is not his own but comes through faith.

3.h: Not that I have obtained it
3.t: Immediately after that, he denies having arrived. Assurance and ongoing struggle sit together in the same paragraph.

4.t: Not an instruction to stop feeling anxious but to redirect it — by prayer, with thanksgiving. The promised result is peace guarding the heart, not the removal of the circumstance.
Contentment is described as learned rather than natural, and in both directions — plenty as well as want. Verse 13 is about enduring circumstances, not achieving ambitions.

1.t: Image of the invisible God, firstborn over all creation, the one in whom all things were created and hold together, the head of the body, the one in whom all fullness dwells. Firstborn here is rank, not birth order — Psalm 89:27 calls David firstborn though he was the youngest son.
Paul says all things were created in him, through him and for him. Greek had words for 'other' and he used neither, which is why insertions at this verse change the argument rather than clarify it.

1.h: Christ in you, the hope of glory
1.t: The mystery hidden for ages and now disclosed. Paul's labour is described as struggling with energy that God supplies.

2.t: The Colossian error added ritual, mystical experience and ascetic rules to Christ. Paul's answer is that all the fullness of deity dwells in him bodily, and that believers have been filled in him — nothing is missing that needs supplementing.
The record of charges against us was nailed to the cross. The image is of a handwritten IOU cancelled.

3.t: The basis of Christian ethics in this letter is not effort but identity: you died, your life is hidden with Christ, therefore live accordingly.

The virtue list is corporate — compassion, kindness, humility, patience, forbearance, forgiveness — and it is held together by love. Verse 16 sets the word of Christ dwelling richly alongside teaching and singing.

4.t: Instruction on speaking to outsiders: wise, gracious, and able to answer each person. Apologetics in one verse, with the manner specified before the content.

1.t: Every other Pauline letter opens with thanksgiving. This one goes straight to astonishment, then to a double curse on anyone preaching another gospel. The stakes are not presented as secondary.
Paul's account of his own calling is given to establish that his gospel was not handed down through Jerusalem. The autobiography is an argument.

2.h: Paul opposes Peter to his face
2.t: Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles when representatives from James arrived. Paul treats table fellowship as a gospel issue rather than a matter of preference, because what Peter's action implied was that Gentile believers were second class.

2.h: Justified by faith, not works of law
2.t: The doctrinal statement of the letter. Verse 20 — crucified with Christ, no longer I who live — is not mysticism but the logic of union with him.

3.t: Paul argues from their own experience of the Spirit, then from Abraham, who was counted righteous before the law existed and before he was circumcised. The chronology does the work.
Christ became a curse for us, quoting Deuteronomy on the man hanged on a tree. Substitution stated as directly as anywhere in Paul.
A statement about standing before God in Christ, and one with consequences the church has been slow to work out. It does not erase distinctions; it denies that they determine status.

4.t: In the fullness of time, God sent his Son; and because we are sons, he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts crying Abba. Both sendings, and adoption as the result.

5.t: The thesis of the second half. Freedom is something to stand in rather than to celebrate abstractly.
The works of the flesh are mostly relational — hostility, strife, jealousy, factions — and so is the fruit of the Spirit. Note it is fruit singular, one cluster, not a menu of gifts.

6.t: Instruction for when a brother is caught in sin: restoration, by those who are spiritual, with gentleness, watching yourself. Then carry each other's burdens — which this group takes as its working description of what brotherhood involves.
Paul's closing, in his own large handwriting. The cross is the only credential he will now claim.

1.t: Not enjoy the trial, but count it — an act of reckoning about what testing produces. James is relentlessly practical from the first paragraph.
The mirror image: a man who looks and immediately forgets what he saw. Hearing without acting is presented as a kind of self-deception rather than a lesser obedience.

2.t: The specific example is seating a rich visitor well and a poor one badly. James calls it judging with evil motives and breaking the royal law.
The apparent clash with Paul dissolves once you see they answer different questions. Paul asks what justifies a sinner before God; James asks what kind of faith is real. Both quote Genesis 15:6.

3.t: A small rudder, a small spark. James's point is not that speech is important but that it is uncontrollable, and that the same mouth blessing God curses people made in his image.
Earthly wisdom is marked by jealousy and selfish ambition; wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle, open to reason. Note that being open to reason is listed as a mark of godliness.

4.t: James traces conflict to desires at war inside people, not to the people they are fighting. Then: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.

5.t: As fierce as anything in Amos, and directed at those who withhold wages from labourers.

5.h: Prayer, and bringing a wanderer back
5.t: The letter ends where it has been heading: prayer in every circumstance, confession to one another, and the recovery of someone who has drifted.

5.h: Prayer for the sick, and when healing does not come
5.t: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the sick person. Christians read this in different ways: as a promise of healing now, as including ultimate resurrection, or as a general principle rather than a guarantee. What is clear is that failure to be healed is never presented in Scripture as proof that someone lacked faith — Paul left Trophimus sick, and his own thorn was not removed. Pray boldly, and never add guilt to someone's illness. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: Two words that set the tone. Chosen by God, and displaced in the world. Peter writes to people for whom the second is a daily experience.
Born again to an inheritance kept in heaven, guarded through faith. The grief of trials is acknowledged in the same breath as the joy — Peter does not choose between them.

2.t: Titles given to Israel at Sinai are applied to a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers. The stone imagery runs through Isaiah and Psalm 118.
Then immediately more than an example: he bore our sins in his body on the tree. Isaiah 53 supplies most of the vocabulary.

3.t: The verse apologetics takes its name from. Note the order: Christ set apart as Lord in the heart first, then readiness, then gentleness and respect. The manner is part of the instruction.

Christ preaching to spirits in prison is among the hardest passages in the New Testament, and the main readings are set out honestly in any good commentary. Nothing in Christian doctrine rests on settling it. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

4.t: Suffering for the name is presented as normal rather than exceptional. Peter's pastoral move is to remove the additional burden of feeling that something has gone wrong.

5.t: Peter writes to elders as a fellow elder, and tells them not to lord it over those entrusted to them. He of all people knew what he had been forgiven.
Grammatically, casting anxiety is how humbling yourself under God's hand is done. Worry is treated as a form of self-reliance.

1.h: What we have heard and touched
1.t: John writes as a witness, against teaching that denied Christ came in a real body. The physicality is deliberate.

1.h: If we say we have no sin
1.t: Written to believers. Confession is presented as ongoing and normal, and the promise is that God is faithful and just — not merely merciful — to forgive.

2.t: Christ as defence counsel with the Father, and as the atoning sacrifice. John's aim in writing is that they would not sin, and his provision is for when they do.

John says Christ is the atoning sacrifice for our sins and also for the sins of the whole world. Reformed Christians have read that as the cross being sufficient for all and effective for those who believe; others read it as an atonement made equally for everyone and applied on condition of faith. The difference is real and it has never stopped either side preaching Christ freely to anyone who will listen. Note the pastoral setting: John raises it to comfort people who have sinned, not to settle a debate. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
Not the created order or its people, but the system organised without God, defined by three desires that pass away.

3.t: See what kind of love — John's word carries astonishment. What we will be has not appeared yet, and the hope purifies now.
Defined by the cross and then measured by whether a man with means shuts his heart against a brother in need. John will not let love stay abstract.

4.t: Not every spiritual claim is from God, and the test given is doctrinal: what is confessed about Jesus come in the flesh.

The most quoted verse in the letter sits inside an argument, and the argument is that love is defined by the cross rather than by our intuitions about it. Verse 10 supplies the definition: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice.

5.t: Older English Bibles include a clause here about three heavenly witnesses. It appears in no Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century and modern translations rightly omit it. Nothing is lost: the Trinity is taught throughout Scripture without it.
The purpose of the whole letter. Assurance is presented as something believers may have, and the three tests running through the letter — belief, obedience, love — are how it is examined.

5.h: Can I know I am saved
5.t: John wrote this letter so that believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance does not rest on feelings, which come and go, but on three things John keeps returning to: believing that Jesus is the Son of God come in the flesh, a real if imperfect desire to obey him, and love for other Christians. The Reformed position is that those truly in Christ will persevere to the end because God keeps them. If you are anxious about whether you are really a Christian, that anxiety is itself worth bringing to someone who knows you. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.h: In the beginning was the Word
1.t: John opens with the first words of Genesis and then says three things: the Word was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. The second and third together rule out both that he is the Father and that he is a lesser being. Everything made was made through him.
Literally, pitched his tent among us — tabernacle language. The glory that filled the tent at Sinai is now in a person.

1.h: No one has ever seen God
1.t: The verse closes the prologue. The same Greek word for God appears twice in it without the article, and translations that render the two differently are making a decision the grammar does not require.

2.t: Roughly a hundred and twenty gallons of wine, at a wedding, from jars used for ceremonial washing. John calls the miracles signs rather than wonders because they point beyond themselves.

John places this at the start where the other Gospels place it at the end. Either there were two, or John has arranged his material thematically. He tells us plainly that the temple Jesus meant was his body.

3.t: The Greek phrase means both 'again' and 'from above', and Nicodemus hears only the first. Jesus' reply about the wind makes the point: the new birth is not something anyone manages.
'So' here means 'in this way' rather than 'so much' — the verse describes the manner of the love, which is the giving of the Son.
John the Baptist's last recorded words, and the cleanest statement of a right attitude to ministry in the New Testament.

4.t: Jesus crosses three barriers in one conversation — ethnic, gender, and moral. Note that he raises her situation directly rather than avoiding it, and that she is the first person in this Gospel he tells plainly that he is the Messiah.
The location of worship becomes irrelevant. God is spirit, and what he seeks is worshippers, which is an arresting way to put it.

5.t: John reports what the hearers understood, and Jesus does not correct them — he goes on to claim to do what the Father does, to give life, and to judge.
They study diligently and miss the point of the study. A warning aimed squarely at people who take the Bible seriously.

6.h: I am the bread of life
6.t: The first of the seven 'I am' statements with a predicate, spoken the day after the feeding and in a discourse about manna.

Our reading is the historic Reformed one: coming to Christ is something the Father enables rather than something we generate, and everyone he gives will in fact come. Other evangelicals read the drawing as a general influence that can be refused. Both sides hold Scripture to be true and are arguing about what it says here. We teach the first, and we say plainly that the second is held by Christians we respect. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

6.h: No one can come unless the Father draws him
6.t: Stated as an inability, not a reluctance. Verse 37 has already said that all the Father gives will come, and John places the two side by side without apology.
A hard saying, and most of the crowd leave. Peter's reply — to whom shall we go — is not enthusiasm but a reasoned conclusion that there is nowhere else.

7.t: Spoken on the last day of the feast when water was ceremonially poured. John explains that he meant the Spirit, not yet given.

8.t: Most modern Bibles set this passage apart with a note, and the BSB does. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts of John, appears in different places in others, and its style differs from the rest of the Gospel. Many scholars think it records a real incident that circulated separately before being placed here. Either way, nothing taught elsewhere in Scripture depends on it, and the flagging is translators being honest rather than hiding something.

8.h: The truth will set you free
8.t: Usually quoted without its condition, which is abiding in his word. The freedom in view is from slavery to sin.
The response — picking up stones — shows how it was understood. The phrase reaches back to Exodus 3 and to the 'I am he' sayings of Isaiah.

9.t: A whole chapter on one healing, structured as a series of interrogations. The man's understanding grows through the chapter while the Pharisees' hardens. It ends with Jesus saying that those who claim to see are the guilty ones.

10.t: Against the background of Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's shepherds and says he will shepherd the flock himself.

10.h: I and the Father are one
10.t: The security of the sheep is stated twice — no one will snatch them from his hand, nor from the Father's — and then the two hands are identified. The crowd's reaction in verse 31 again shows what they heard.

11.h: I am the resurrection and the life
11.t: Said to a grieving woman before the miracle, and it reframes her hope from a distant event to a present person.
The shortest verse, and theologically among the heaviest: he is about to raise the man and he weeps anyway. Grief is not a failure of faith.

12.t: John quotes Isaiah 6 — the temple vision — and says Isaiah spoke about him. The subject through this passage does not change: the one not believed in, the one Isaiah spoke of, the one the rulers believed in.

13.t: The foot-washing is introduced by saying that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands — and what he did with that knowledge was wash feet.
New in its measure: as I have loved you. The mark by which outsiders are to identify his disciples is how they treat each other.

14.h: The way, the truth and the life
14.t: Exclusive, and spoken as comfort to frightened men rather than as a slogan.
Philip's request and Jesus' reply. As direct a statement of his relation to the Father as the Gospel contains.
'Another of the same kind' — the Spirit is presented as a helper like Jesus himself, not a different order of thing.

15.t: Abiding is the whole instruction. Fruit is the result rather than the aim, and apart from him the yield is stated as nothing, not as less.

16.t: He convicts, guides into truth, and glorifies the Son. Verse 14 is decisive for how we pray: the Spirit's own work is to point away from himself and toward Christ.

17.t: Jesus prays for himself, for the Twelve, and then for everyone who would believe through their message — which includes the reader. The requested unity in verse 21 is patterned on the unity of Father and Son.

18.h: My kingdom is not of this world
18.t: Not that it has nothing to do with this world, but that its origin and method are elsewhere — which is why, he says, his servants are not fighting.

19.t: One word in Greek, tetelestai, used on receipts to mean 'paid in full'. It is a statement of completion, not defeat.
John stops the narrative to insist that he saw it. The detail matters to him because it establishes a real death against those who denied it.

20.t: Thomas addresses Jesus directly with both titles, and Jesus accepts it and pronounces a blessing on those who believe without seeing. It is the climax of the Gospel's argument.
John states his purpose: that you may believe, and believing have life. Everything selected was selected for that.

21.t: Peter denied three times and is asked three times. Jesus does not extract an apology; he gives him work to do. The restoration is public because the failure was.

1.t: Not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God's power for salvation; in it a righteousness from God is revealed, from faith to faith. These two verses set the agenda for the letter and for the Reformation.

1.h: The case against the pagan world
1.t: Paul argues that what may be known about God is plain from creation, so that people are without excuse. The downward sequence — knowing, not honouring, exchanging, being given over — is repeated three times.

This is a subject men are regularly asked about, so it is worth being clear and kind at the same time. The historic teaching of the church, across every major tradition and still held by the great majority of Christians worldwide, is that sexual intimacy belongs within marriage between a man and a woman. Paul's point in this passage is that when people turn from God, desire becomes disordered — and he immediately goes on in chapter 2 to say that everyone who judges others is guilty too. Some recent scholars read these verses as addressing only exploitative practices of Paul's day; most evangelical and Reformed scholars have not found that persuasive. Whatever the question, no one is more sinful than anyone else, every person is made in God's image and deserves dignity, and 1 Corinthians 6:11 — 'such were some of you' — is the note the gospel always sounds. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

2.t: Having secured the agreement of his religious readers, Paul turns the argument on them. The one who judges does the same things.

3.t: A chain of Old Testament quotations establishing universal guilt. The law's function here is to stop mouths and give knowledge of sin, not to provide a route out.

The turn of the letter. Justified freely by his grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation — so that God is both just and the justifier. The problem being solved is how a just God can acquit the guilty without ceasing to be just.

4.t: Counted righteous by faith before circumcision and centuries before the law. Paul uses the chronology to show that faith-righteousness was never a later arrangement.

5.t: Justification produces peace, access, and hope — and Paul immediately runs it through suffering, which produces endurance, character, hope.
Adam and Christ as heads of two humanities. The logic of imputation is here: condemnation through one, justification through one.

6.t: Paul raises the objection his own doctrine invites and answers it with union: we died with Christ and were raised with him. Baptism pictures it.

6.h: What baptism means, and what Christians dispute
6.t: All agree it marks union with Christ in his death and resurrection. Two things are argued: who should be baptised, and how. Baptist churches baptise those who profess faith, by immersion; Presbyterian, Anglican and Reformed paedobaptist churches also baptise the children of believers, usually by pouring. Both appeal to covenant and to apostolic practice. It is a real difference and not a trivial one, but it has never been a boundary of the faith itself. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
The contrast is exact. Wages are earned; the gift is not.

7.t: Paul is careful to protect the law's goodness while denying it can save. The problem is not the standard but us.

Interpreters divide on whether Paul describes his pre-Christian experience or his present one. The strongest reading takes it as the believer's ongoing struggle, which is why the passage has comforted so many. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

8.t: The verdict, stated first. Everything in the chapter flows from it.
