The Spirit indwells, gives life, leads, and testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. The cry Abba appears here as in Galatians 4.

8.h: When we do not know what to pray
8.t: The Spirit intercedes with groans words cannot carry, and God who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. A person is being described, not an influence.
The golden chain of verses 29–30 runs foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified — with no attrition at any link. The chapter ends in one of the great passages of Scripture.

This verse is often quoted too quickly to people in pain. It does not say everything is good, or that suffering is not real. It says that God works in all things for the good of those who love him — and verse 29 defines that good as being made like Christ. Scripture never gives a full explanation for why particular suffering happens; Job is told a great deal about God and nothing about the reasons. What it gives is the cross, where God himself suffered, and the promise of verse 18 that present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come. If you are grieving, lament first; the explanation can wait. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

9.t: He would be cut off himself if it would save his own people. Whatever is said in this chapter is said by a man in anguish, not in detachment.

9.h: The chapter Christians argue over most
9.t: We take Paul to be teaching that God's choice of individuals rests on his mercy rather than on anything foreseen in them, which is the Reformed reading and the one this group holds; the Westminster Confession 3.5 states it directly, that God chose his people without any foresight of faith or works in them. Others read the chapter as concerning nations and roles in redemptive history rather than eternal destinies, or as election based on foreseen faith. Paul anticipates the objection in verse 19 and does not soften it, which is itself worth weighing. Hold the doctrine the way Paul does here — alongside the grief of verses 1 to 3. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

Paul does not soften the difficulty; he states the objection sharply and answers with God's freedom in mercy. The potter and clay image comes from Jeremiah. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

10.t: One argument running through six verses: confess Jesus as Lord, call on the Lord, believe in the one called upon. The Lord confessed in verse 9 and the Lord called on in verse 13 are the same Lord, and verse 13 is a quotation from Joel about God.
The logic of mission stated as a chain of questions. Faith comes from hearing.

11.t: Paul's answer to whether God has rejected Israel is no — using himself as exhibit one.

11.h: Is there a future for Israel
11.t: Paul says a hardening has come on Israel in part, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and then all Israel will be saved. What that means is debated: a large-scale future turning of Jewish people to Christ, or the sum of elect Jews and Gentiles across history, or the church as the true Israel. The first has been the most common reading in the Reformed tradition and is probably the most natural here. The text does not settle it as tightly as either side usually claims. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
Three chapters of the hardest material in Paul end not in a conclusion but in worship. That is itself instructive.

12.t: The hinge from doctrine to life. In view of God's mercies — everything in chapters 1 to 11 — offer your bodies. Worship is defined as the whole of life.

A rapid series of instructions on life together: devoted in brotherly love, honouring one another, joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer, practising hospitality. This group takes verses 10 to 13 as a description of what it is trying to be.

13.t: Written under Nero, which should govern how comfortable anyone feels quoting it. Paul's point is the legitimacy of civil order, not the goodness of particular rulers.
Not replaces it — fulfils it. Paul lists commandments and then sums them.

14.t: Paul's category for issues where believers may genuinely differ. The instruction is not to despise or judge, and the aim is that each is convinced in his own mind. Note verse 11 quotes the same Isaiah oath that Philippians 2 applies to Christ.

15.h: Bear with the failings of the weak
15.t: Christ did not please himself. Verses 5 to 7 — endurance, encouragement, one mind and one voice, accept one another as Christ accepted you — is one of the passages this group returns to.
Paul's ambition was to preach where Christ was not known. It explains most of his travel decisions.

16.t: Twenty-six people named, roughly a third of them women, including Phoebe who probably carried the letter. It is the best surviving picture of what an early congregation looked like.

1.t: No argument for God's existence is offered anywhere in Scripture; it begins by assuming it. The verse also rules out matter being eternal and God being part of creation.

1.h: How Christians read the six days
1.t: What this chapter teaches is not in dispute among Christians: God created everything out of nothing, deliberately, in order, and called it good, with humanity made last and in his image. How long it took is disputed, and honestly so. Some read the days as ordinary days; some as long ages; some as a literary framework arranging the acts of creation rather than timing them. All three are held by people who take Scripture as God's word. We would not make any of them a test of fellowship, and we would be cautious of anyone who does. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

The plural has been read as majestic, as divine council, and as an early hint of plurality in God. Whichever, the image is given to humanity as male and female together, and it carries a commission: fill, subdue, rule — the first job description.
The repeated refrain becomes emphatic at the end. Whatever is wrong with the world now, the text is clear it was not made wrong.

2.t: Humanity is made of the ground and animated by God's own breath. Both halves matter, and the Bible never treats the body as the regrettable part.

We hold that he was, and that this is not a side issue. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 sets one man's disobedience against one man's obedience, and it is hard to see how the comparison works if only one of the two ever existed. Some evangelical scholars now read Adam as representative rather than as the first individual; we think that costs more than it saves. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
The first thing declared not good in a very good creation is a man on his own. The word for the woman means a corresponding strength, not a subordinate — it is used elsewhere of God himself.

3.t: The serpent's method is to question, then to contradict, then to reframe God's motive as self-protective. The sin is presented as a bid for autonomy rather than an appetite for fruit.
Shame, hiding, and then blame passed along the chain. The consequences are relational before they are anything else.
The offspring of the woman will crush the serpent's head and be struck in the heel. Christian readers have seen the whole gospel in outline here since the earliest centuries.

4.t: Sin is described as crouching at the door, desiring him. The question 'am I my brother's keeper' is left unanswered by God and answered by the rest of Scripture.

6.t: The diagnosis is total and internal. God's grief in verse 6 is stated without embarrassment. Noah found favour — the first appearance of grace in the Bible.
Righteous and blameless among the people of his time — and the ark's dimensions are given precisely, as if to say this was a real object.

9.t: The reason given for the seriousness of murder is the image, which grounds human dignity in something other than capacity or usefulness.

11.t: A tower to make a name for themselves, and the scattering that follows. Acts 2 deliberately reverses it.
He leaves Ur for Canaan and settles halfway, at Haran. The call to Abram in chapter 12 finishes a journey his father abandoned.

12.t: Land, people, and blessing to all the families of the earth. Paul calls the last clause the gospel announced in advance. Everything from here to Revelation is this promise being worked out.
Three verses after the promise, he lies about his wife to save himself. Genesis never cleans up its heroes.

15.t: Abraham believed God and it was credited to him. Both Paul and James build on this verse; it is the seed of the doctrine of justification.
In the covenant ceremony both parties should pass between the pieces. Only God does. He takes the whole obligation on himself.

22.t: The hardest chapter in Genesis. Note the phrase 'God will provide for himself the lamb', the substitute caught in the thicket, and that the place is named 'the LORD will provide' — on a mountain in Moriah, where the temple would later stand.

22.h: Why would God ask Abraham to do this
22.t: This is one of the hardest chapters in Scripture and it is right to find it disturbing. Three things help. First, the reader is told at the outset it is a test, and God stops it; child sacrifice is condemned elsewhere in the law as detestable, so the chapter is not endorsing it. Second, Abraham tells his servants that he and the boy will both come back, and Hebrews 11:19 says he reasoned God could raise the dead. Third, the substitute is provided on the very mountain where the temple would stand, and 'God will provide the lamb' is fulfilled when the Father does not spare his own Son. The chapter points beyond itself. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

50.t: Joseph's summary of the whole narrative and one of the clearest statements in Scripture of how God's sovereignty and human responsibility operate together. Both intentions are real; only one prevails.

5.h: The genealogy that ends in death
5.t: Eight times the refrain: and he died. The exception is Enoch, who walked with God and was not. Genesis is establishing the reach of chapter 3.

7.t: Note that God shuts the door. The narrative is careful to say the waters covered the mountains and that everything with the breath of life died.

8.h: A new start, with the same problem
8.t: God's promise never to destroy the earth this way again is given because the human heart is evil from youth — the same reason given for the flood in 6:5. Mercy is not conditional on improvement.

16.t: The God who sees. She is the first person in Scripture to give God a name, and she is an Egyptian slave woman.

17.t: The covenant sign given to Abraham. Paul's argument in Romans 4 depends on the fact that he was already counted righteous before this chapter.

18.t: Down from fifty to ten. The audacity is remarkable and God does not rebuke it, which says something about what prayer is permitted to sound like.

19.t: Grim reading. Ezekiel 16:49 names the city's sin as arrogance and refusing to help the poor and needy, alongside the events here. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

21.t: Isaac means 'he laughs'. Sarah laughed in disbelief in chapter 18 and laughs in joy here; the name holds both.

25.t: Esau despised his birthright. Hebrews 12:16 uses him as the warning example of trading something permanent for something immediate.

28.t: Jacob is running away after deceiving his father, and God appears and makes promises to him anyway. Jesus applies this image to himself in John 1:51.

32.t: All night, and Jacob will not let go without a blessing. He leaves with a new name and a permanent limp, which is about right.

37.t: The coat, the dreams, the brothers' hatred. The narrative turns on human wickedness that God will later say he meant for good.

39.t: Joseph does the right thing and is imprisoned for it. The refrain four times is that the LORD was with him — including in prison.

45.t: The reconciliation. He weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it, and tells them not to be distressed because God sent him ahead to preserve life.

13.t: Having been promised the land, he lets his nephew pick. Lot chooses by what looks well watered and ends up near Sodom.

14.t: A priest-king of Salem with no genealogy given. Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 both build on that silence.

20.t: Abraham repeats the deception about Sarah. Genesis reports his relapses as flatly as his faith.

24.t: The longest chapter in Genesis, and almost all of it is a servant praying and then telling the story of his prayer being answered.

27.t: Rebekah engineers it, Jacob executes it, Isaac cannot undo it. Nobody in the chapter behaves well and God's promise runs through it anyway.

29.t: The man who impersonated his brother wakes up married to the wrong sister. The narrator does not comment; he does not need to.

33.t: Jacob expects four hundred men and gets an embrace. Twenty years of dread resolved in a sentence.

41.h: From the dungeon to second in Egypt
41.t: Joseph credits the interpretation to God before he gives it. The rise is sudden and the waiting was thirteen years.

42.t: They do not recognise him. Joseph's harshness here is usually read as testing whether they have changed.

49.t: Jacob's blessing on his fourth son, and the line the Messiah is expected to come through.

10.t: Seventy nations descended from Noah's sons. The list is theological as much as ethnographic: every people on earth comes from one family, which is the ground for the promise in 12:3 that all of them will be blessed.

23.t: Abraham, promised the whole land, owns exactly one field of it at his death — bought at full price to bury Sarah. Hebrews 11 says he died still waiting, and this chapter shows it.

26.t: The only chapter about Isaac as the main figure. He repeats his father's lie about his wife and reopens his father's wells. Faith is shown passing down a generation, flaws included.

30.t: Rachel and Leah compete through children and servants, and Jacob's flocks multiply through a breeding scheme. God works through a family behaving badly, without endorsing any of it.

31.t: Twenty years of sharp dealing on both sides end with a boundary heap and a treaty. Rachel's theft of the household gods shows how incomplete the family's faith still was.

34.t: A grim chapter of violation and brutal revenge. The text reports it without approval, and Jacob's deathbed words in chapter 49 condemn Simeon and Levi for it. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

35.t: Jacob orders the foreign gods buried before returning to where God first met him. Renewal begins with putting things away.

36.t: A full chapter for the brother outside the line of promise. Genesis does not forget him, and Edom's story runs on through the prophets.

38.t: An uncomfortable interruption in the Joseph story. Judah's line — the line of David and the Messiah — continues through Tamar, whom Matthew names in Jesus' genealogy. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

40.t: Joseph credits God before interpreting the dreams, then asks to be remembered. The cupbearer forgets for two full years.

43.t: Judah offers himself as surety for Benjamin — the first sign that the brother who sold Joseph has changed.

44.t: The longest speech in Genesis, offering himself as a slave in Benjamin's place. It is the moment Joseph can no longer hold back, and a picture of substitution.

46.h: Do not be afraid to go down
46.t: God speaks to Jacob at Beersheba and promises to go with him into Egypt and bring him back. The family moves under promise, not in exile.

47.t: He buys up the land and people for Pharaoh in exchange for food. Readers are divided on whether this is presented as wise administration or as the beginning of the slavery Exodus opens with.

48.t: Jacob blesses the younger grandson above the elder, deliberately. The pattern of God choosing the unexpected runs right through Genesis.

1.t: Two ways, two ends. Placed first deliberately: the whole collection is to be read as instruction, not only as prayer.

2.t: A royal psalm quoted more in the New Testament than almost any other. Verse 7 is spoken at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration.

8.t: Opens and closes with the same line. Hebrews 2 applies the middle of it to Christ.
The question arises from looking at the sky, not from introspection. Hebrews 2 applies the answer to Christ.

16.h: You will not abandon me to Sheol
16.t: Peter quotes this at Pentecost, arguing that David spoke it of the Messiah because David's own tomb was still there.
In your presence is fullness of joy. Peter quotes verses 8 to 11 at Pentecost.

19.t: Creation speaks without words; the law speaks with them. The psalm moves from the sky to Scripture to the psalmist's own hidden faults.

19.h: Let the words of my mouth
19.t: The prayer that many preachers still use before speaking, and it comes at the end of a psalm about the heavens and the law.

22.t: The line Jesus quotes from the cross. The psalm describes pierced hands and feet, divided garments and casting lots, then turns at verse 22 to vindication and worldwide worship.
Written centuries before crucifixion was practised. Bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaw, garments divided by lot — all quoted at the cross.

23.t: The most familiar psalm in the world, and note that the valley is walked through rather than avoided, and that the table is set in the presence of enemies rather than after their defeat.
Not around it, and the pronouns change here from 'he' to 'you'. The psalmist stops describing God and starts speaking to him.

32.t: Paul quotes this in Romans 4 as evidence of righteousness credited apart from works. Verses 3 and 4 describe the physical effects of unconfessed sin with unusual precision.
God speaking in the middle of a psalm about confession. Forgiveness leads to guidance, in that order.

42.t: Thirst as the image for longing. The psalmist's tears have been his food and he preaches to his own soul.
The psalmist talks to himself rather than merely listening to himself, which is the practical move the psalm teaches.

46.t: Though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the sea. The refuge is named before the crisis is described.

Often read as an invitation to quiet reflection; in context it is closer to 'stop' — addressed to raging nations, not to anxious individuals. It comforts for a different reason than people usually think.

51.t: The model penitential psalm. Note verse 4 — against you only have I sinned — and that what God is said to want is a broken spirit rather than sacrifice.

51.h: Create in me a pure heart
51.t: The verb is the one used in Genesis 1 for creating out of nothing. David is not asking for repair.

73.t: The most honest treatment of envy in Scripture. The psalmist nearly loses his footing over the prosperity of the wicked, and what changes is not his circumstances but his vantage point.

73.h: Whom have I in heaven but you
73.t: My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart. Written by a man who had almost lost his footing.

90.t: From everlasting to everlasting you are God. Moses' psalm opens with permanence before describing how short life is.

90.h: Teach us to number our days
90.t: Attributed to Moses, the oldest psalm in the collection, and the only sensible response to its own bleak arithmetic.

103.h: Bless the LORD, O my soul
103.t: A catalogue of benefits, and then verse 14 — he remembers that we are dust. The tenderness of that is easy to miss.

103.h: As far as the east is from the west
103.t: A distance with no measure, unlike north and south which meet at the poles.

110.h: The LORD said to my Lord
110.t: The most frequently quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. Jesus uses it himself to press the question of how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord.
In the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews builds several chapters on this half-verse.

119.t: An acrostic of twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, each stanza beginning with a successive Hebrew letter. Almost every verse mentions God's word under one of eight terms. The form is a discipline, not decoration.
Enough light for the next step rather than the whole road, which is how guidance usually arrives.

130.t: With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared — not that you may be taken lightly. Forgiveness produces reverence rather than casualness.
My soul waits for the Lord. Luther called this one of the Pauline psalms.

139.t: Omniscience, omnipresence and creation applied personally rather than abstractly. It ends by inviting the searching it began by describing.

139.h: Knit together in my mother's womb
139.t: All my days were written before one of them came to be.

150.t: The Psalter has run through lament, protest, doubt and despair, and it ends in unqualified praise. The order is the argument.

3.t: The superscription places this during Absalom's rebellion. He lies down and sleeps anyway.

6.t: Worn out from groaning, drenching the bed with tears. Scripture does not require composure.

13.t: Four 'how longs', then two requests, then trust. The shape of nearly every lament, in six verses.

27.t: Confidence and fear side by side in one psalm. It ends with wait for the LORD, repeated, which suggests nothing had yet resolved.

34.t: That the LORD is good. Peter quotes this psalm in his first letter.
And he saves the crushed in spirit. Verse 8 — taste and see — comes from the same psalm.

37.t: Three times. The counsel is to trust, delight, commit and be still, which is harder than it reads.

40.t: He put a new song in my mouth. Paul's language about rescue has this psalm behind it.

63.t: Written in the wilderness. Your love is better than life — an extraordinary sentence from a man with no water.

84.t: A pilgrim psalm. The valley of weeping becomes a place of springs for those passing through it.

84.h: Better one day in your courts
84.t: Than a thousand elsewhere. The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper.

88.h: The one that does not turn
88.t: Almost alone among the laments, this one never resolves. It ends in darkness. God left it in, which is the most pastorally useful fact about it.

91.h: He who dwells in the shelter
91.t: Quoted by Satan at the temptation, which is a caution about lifting promises out of context.

100.h: Know that the LORD is God
100.t: Seven imperatives in five verses. It is we who are his, and not we ourselves who made us.

116.t: Because he heard. A thanksgiving psalm after deliverance from death, with the honest admission in verse 11 that he said in his alarm that everyone is a liar.

121.t: A song of ascents, sung going up to Jerusalem. He who watches over you will not slumber — said six times in eight verses.

127.t: Work without God is described as anxious toil. The second half gives sleep to those he loves.

133.t: Three verses on the good of brotherhood, pictured as oil running down Aaron's beard. As close to a text for this group as the Psalter gets.

145.t: The LORD is good to all, and his compassion is over all he has made. An acrostic psalm of praise.

15.t: A short catalogue of ordinary integrity — keeping an oath even when it hurts, lending without interest.

25.t: An acrostic psalm of guidance, with the admission in verse 16 that he is lonely and afflicted.

30.h: Weeping may stay for the night
30.t: Rejoicing comes in the morning. Written for the dedication of the temple and still used at funerals.

33.h: By the word of the LORD
33.t: The heavens were made. Creation by speech, picked up in John 1 and Hebrews 11.
Whose God is the LORD. Often applied to modern countries; written about the people God chose.

62.t: Repeated at the start and the middle. Verse 8 — pour out your hearts to him — is the instruction the psalm is modelling.

65.t: An agricultural psalm about rain, pastures and hills clothed with gladness. Not every psalm is about crisis.

77.t: The turn of the psalm is a deliberate act of memory. He stops asking and starts recounting.

86.t: Teach me your way that I may rely on your faithfulness. One of the best short prayers in the Psalter.

95.h: Today, if you hear his voice
95.t: Quoted at length in Hebrews 3 and 4, introduced there as the Holy Spirit speaking.

96.t: Declare his glory among the nations. Missionary theology centuries before the Great Commission.

102.t: Addressed to the LORD here, and applied to the Son in Hebrews 1:10–12.

107.t: Wanderers, prisoners, the sick and sailors, each with the refrain: then they cried to the LORD in their trouble. Verse 29 — he stilled the storm — is what the disciples would have known.

115.h: Those who make idols will be like them
115.t: A sharp little argument: idols have mouths that cannot speak, and their makers become as lifeless as what they worship.

118.t: Quoted by Jesus of himself, and by Peter before the Sanhedrin. The most cited psalm verse in the New Testament after 110:1.

118.h: This is the day the LORD has made
118.t: In context, the day of an unexpected deliverance rather than any day in general.

126.t: Those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy. A song of ascents for people returning from exile.

131.t: Three verses. The image is of a child no longer crying for what it wants, simply content to be held.

138.h: The LORD will fulfil his purpose
138.t: He will not abandon the works of his hands. Confidence grounded in God's character rather than circumstances.

143.t: Word of your unfailing love, for I have put my trust in you. A psalm for starting the day badly.

146.h: Do not put your trust in princes
146.t: Their plans come to nothing on the day they die. A necessary corrective in every generation.

4.h: In peace I will lie down
4.t: You alone make me dwell in safety. An evening psalm, and the companion to Psalm 3's morning.

5.h: In the morning I lay my requests
5.t: And wait expectantly. The waiting is named as part of the praying.

7.h: Bring to an end the violence
7.t: You who probe minds and hearts. Justice asked for by someone who accepts being examined himself.

9.t: Those who know your name trust in you. Knowing the name means knowing the character.

10.h: Why do you stand far off
10.t: The psalm asks it without apology and spends most of its length describing the wicked before turning.

11.t: What can the righteous do? The answer given is that the LORD is in his holy temple — a change of vantage rather than of circumstance.

12.t: Like silver refined seven times, set against the flattering lips of verse 2.

14.h: The fool says in his heart
14.t: There is no God. Paul quotes this psalm at length in Romans 3.

17.t: Hide me in the shadow of your wings. Two images of close protection in one verse.

18.t: Rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold. Six metaphors before the psalm has properly begun.

20.t: But we trust in the name of the LORD our God. A war psalm that names the actual security.

21.t: A royal psalm, and the New Testament reads this line of psalms as pointing beyond David.

24.t: Clean hands and a pure heart. The psalm ends with the gates lifting for the King of glory.

26.t: Examine my heart and my mind. Few psalms invite scrutiny this directly.

28.t: The LORD is my strength and my shield. The turn comes at verse 6, after six verses of pleading.

29.t: Seven times, over the waters, breaking cedars, shaking the desert. A storm psalm that ends in the temple.

31.t: I commit my spirit — the words Jesus spoke from the cross.

35.t: An imprecatory psalm. Note the psalmist asks God to act rather than acting himself, which is the model. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

36.h: Your love reaches to the heavens
36.t: In your light we see light. The psalm moves from the wickedness of sin to the breadth of God's love in three verses.

38.t: Physical description of guilt — no soundness in my body, wounds festering. The body keeps the account.

39.h: Show me the measure of my days
39.t: Let me know how fleeting my life is. Honest about mortality in a way modern religion rarely is.

41.t: Has lifted up his heel against me. Jesus quotes it of Judas.

43.t: The continuation of Psalm 42; the two were probably one psalm. The refrain closes both.

44.t: Why do you sleep? A communal lament that accuses God of forgetting, and it is in Scripture.

45.t: A wedding psalm for a king, quoted in Hebrews 1 and applied to the Son.

47.t: God reigns over the nations — one of the psalms that refuses to keep God local.

48.h: This God is our God for ever
48.t: He will be our guide even to the end. The psalm walks round Jerusalem's walls and towers, then concludes that the real security was never the fortifications but the God who dwells there.

49.t: When someone grows rich, for they will take nothing with them. Ecclesiastes in miniature.

50.h: The cattle on a thousand hills
50.t: God says that if he were hungry he would not tell us. An argument against thinking worship supplies him something.

52.t: Flourishing in the house of God, set against the man who trusted in his wealth.

53.t: With minor variations. The Psalter preserves both, which tells you something about how it was assembled.

55.h: If an enemy were insulting me
55.t: But it is you, a man like myself, my companion. Betrayal by a friend, described precisely.

56.h: You keep track of my sorrows
56.t: Record my misery, list my tears on your scroll. An extraordinary image of being noticed.

57.h: In the shadow of your wings
57.t: Until the disaster has passed. Written in a cave, according to the superscription.

59.h: I will sing of your strength
59.t: In the morning I will sing of your love, for you are my fortress. Written while his house was being watched.

61.h: The rock that is higher than I
61.t: Lead me to it — an admission that he cannot get there himself.

66.h: If I had cherished sin in my heart
66.t: The Lord would not have listened. A sobering verse about unanswered prayer.

67.h: That your ways may be known
67.t: The blessing asked for is so that it reaches the nations. Mission built into a benediction.

68.t: God sets the lonely in families. Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4.

69.t: Quoted by the disciples when Jesus cleared the temple. The psalm is quoted in the New Testament more than most.

71.h: Do not cast me away when I am old
71.t: A psalm of a man past his strength, still asking to declare God's power to the next generation.

72.h: A king who defends the afflicted
72.t: Solomon's psalm, and the standard by which every later king was measured and found wanting.

75.t: No one from the east or west can exalt a man; God brings one down and lifts another up.

78.t: A long retelling of Israel's history so that children would put their trust in God and not forget.

80.t: Make your face shine on us. The refrain appears three times, each time more urgent.

81.t: And I will fill it — followed by the lament that Israel would not listen.

85.t: Righteousness and peace kiss each other. Four attributes personified in one line.

89.h: I will sing of the LORD's great love
89.t: A psalm about the covenant with David that ends, forty verses later, asking where that love has gone.

92.h: They will still bear fruit in old age
92.t: Planted in the house of the LORD. A sabbath psalm.

93.t: Mightier than the thunder of the great waters. Four verses, all about stability.

94.h: When anxiety was great within me
94.t: Your consolation brought me joy. A verse worth knowing by heart.

97.h: Let those who love the LORD hate evil
97.t: Love and hatred held together as one instruction.

98.t: The psalm behind 'Joy to the World'. The rivers clap and the mountains sing.

99.t: The threefold 'he is holy' in this psalm anticipates Isaiah 6.

101.t: In my own house — and set no vile thing before my eyes. A psalm about private integrity.

104.t: Following the order of Genesis 1. Verse 15 mentions wine that gladdens human hearts without embarrassment.

105.t: Israel's history retold with the emphasis on God's faithfulness rather than their failure — the opposite emphasis to Psalm 106.

106.t: Same history, told as a catalogue of rebellion. The Psalter puts both versions side by side on purpose.

111.t: The beginning of wisdom. An acrostic psalm, paired with 112.

112.t: His heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD. Not the absence of bad news, but of dread about it.

113.h: He raises the poor from the dust
113.t: Hannah's song and Mary's both draw on this psalm.

117.t: Two verses, addressed to all nations. Paul quotes it in Romans 15 as evidence the Gentiles were always in view.

120.h: I call on the LORD in my distress
120.t: The first of the fifteen songs of ascents, sung going up to Jerusalem.

122.h: I rejoiced with those who said
122.t: Let us go to the house of the LORD. A pilgrim's psalm about being glad to go.

123.t: Look to the hand of their master, so our eyes look to the LORD. Watching for a signal.

124.h: Our help is in the name of the LORD
124.t: The maker of heaven and earth. Used as an opening sentence in churches for centuries.

125.t: So the LORD surrounds his people. The geography is the argument.

128.h: Blessed are all who fear the LORD
128.t: Ordinary domestic blessing — food from your labour, a family round the table.

129.h: They have not gained the victory
129.t: A psalm of a people who have been ploughed over and are still there.

132.t: A psalm about bringing the ark to Jerusalem and about God's promise in return.

134.t: Three verses, addressed to those who minister by night in the house of the LORD.

135.h: Those who make them will be like them
135.t: The same argument as Psalm 115: you become what you worship.

136.t: Twenty-six times. Designed to be sung antiphonally, and the repetition is the point rather than a flaw.

137.t: It begins in grief and ends with a line about dashing infants on rocks. Honest rage handed to God rather than acted on.

137.h: Can a Christian pray a psalm like this
137.t: These verses are among the most shocking in the Bible. They are the honest cry of people who had watched their own children killed by Babylon, and the psalmist takes that rage to God instead of acting on it. The Psalms model bringing every emotion to God, including ones we should not act out. Christians read these psalms through the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies, and through God's promise that vengeance belongs to him. The appropriate response is not to pray the words against people we dislike, but to learn from them that God can bear the full weight of our anger and that justice is safe in his hands. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

140.h: The LORD secures justice for the poor
140.t: The conclusion of a psalm asking for protection from violent men.

141.h: Set a guard over my mouth
141.t: And verse 5: let a righteous man strike me, it is a kindness. A prayer to be corrected.

142.h: No one cares for my life
142.t: Written in the cave. The loneliest sentence in the Psalter.

144.h: What is mankind that you care
144.t: A fleeting breath, a passing shadow. The psalm still ends asking for blessing.

147.t: And determines the number of the stars, in consecutive verses. The Psalter refuses to separate the cosmic from the personal.

148.t: Angels, sun, sea creatures, weather, mountains, kings and children. A comprehensive summons.

149.t: Praise combined with a two-edged sword. The psalm is used carefully in Christian tradition, and should be.

54.t: Written when the Ziphites betrayed David's location to Saul. The psalm is four verses of plea and three of confidence.

58.h: Break the teeth of the wicked
58.t: An imprecatory psalm against corrupt rulers. The psalmist asks God to act rather than acting himself, and the aim is that people will say there is a God who judges. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

60.t: With God we will gain the victory. Written after a defeat.

64.t: A psalm about slander and plotting words, ending with God's arrow turning their own tongues against them.

70.t: Come quickly to me. Almost identical to the end of Psalm 40.

74.h: Why have you rejected us for ever
74.t: A lament over the destroyed temple. The psalmist reminds God of creation and of his covenant, arguing from God's own record.

76.t: Even the anger of men is turned to serve God's purposes.

79.t: Grief over Jerusalem's destruction, asking for help for the sake of God's name rather than Israel's merit.

82.t: A difficult psalm. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10. Interpreters divide over whether the 'gods' are human judges or heavenly beings. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

83.t: The psalm asks for the enemies to be shamed so that they will seek God's name and know he is Most High.

87.t: Egypt, Babylon, Philistia and Tyre recorded as born there. Nations counted as citizens of God's city — a startling Old Testament picture.

108.t: Parts of Psalm 57 and Psalm 60 combined into one. The Psalter reuses its own material.

109.t: A sustained curse on a false accuser. Peter applies verse 8 to Judas. Read as honest rage entrusted to God, not a pattern for our own speech. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

114.t: A short, vivid poem on the exodus. The mountains skip like rams at the presence of God.

1.t: Three sets of fourteen, tying Jesus to Abraham and David. Four women appear in it — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — each with an irregular story, and each a reminder that this line runs through grace rather than respectability.
Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins; Immanuel, God with us. Matthew opens and closes his Gospel on that second idea — compare 28:20.

2.t: Gentile astrologers find him while the chief priests, who correctly quote the prophecy, stay home. Matthew's irony is deliberate.
Matthew reads Israel's history as being recapitulated in Jesus: down to Egypt, out again, through water, into the wilderness.

3.t: John's objection is reasonable. Jesus answers that it is to fulfil all righteousness — identifying himself with the people he came to save. The Father speaks and the Spirit descends.

4.t: Every reply Jesus gives is from Deuteronomy, from the very chapters about Israel's wilderness failures. He succeeds at the points where they fell.

5.t: Not entry requirements but a description of the people God blesses — and the list is comprehensively the opposite of what any culture rewards.
Jesus claims to fulfil the law rather than replace it, and then sets a standard exceeding that of the Pharisees, which would have sounded impossible.

5.h: Which Old Testament laws still apply
5.t: Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. The historic Reformed way of reading this distinguishes three kinds of law: the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still binds; the ceremonial law of sacrifices, food and cleanness, which is fulfilled in Christ and no longer practised (Hebrews and Acts 15); and the civil law of Israel as a nation, whose principles of justice remain instructive but which is not a code for modern states. Not every Christian tradition uses these categories, but the conclusion is widely shared. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

5.h: You have heard… but I say
5.t: Six times. He is not correcting Moses but going behind the external rule to the heart, and claiming the authority to do it.

6.t: Six petitions in two halves: three about God's name, kingdom and will, then three about our bread, forgiveness and protection. The order is the lesson.
Three arguments — the birds, the lilies, and the futility of the anxiety itself. The instruction ends with seeking the kingdom first, which is the actual remedy.

7.t: Almost always quoted without verse 5, which assumes you will eventually help with the speck — after dealing with the plank.
The chapter closes with people who prophesied and cast out demons being told he never knew them. Matthew puts the most frightening verses in the Sermon at the end of it.

8.t: A Gentile soldier understands authority better than Israel does, and Jesus says so plainly.

9.t: He records his own story in a single verse and moves on. The quotation from Hosea — I desire mercy, not sacrifice — is used twice in this Gospel.

10.t: The hardest saying in the chapter. It is a statement about the effect of allegiance to Christ on families, not an endorsement of conflict.

11.t: The man who identified him at the Jordan sends from prison to ask whether he is the one. Jesus does not rebuke the question, and then calls John the greatest born of women.
The gentlest invitation in the Gospels, and it sits immediately after some of the sternest warnings.

13.t: The kingdom described as hidden, small, mixed, and immensely valuable. Note that several of them assume growth alongside opposition rather than instead of it.

16.t: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. Interpreters divide over whether the rock is Peter, his confession, or Christ; what is not in doubt is that the church is Christ's and that he builds it.
An instrument of execution, to people who had seen them used. The metaphor has been softened by familiarity.

18.t: A process in three stages, aimed throughout at winning the brother rather than removing him. Verse 20 is about this context, not about prayer meeting attendance.
The parable that follows makes the arithmetic irrelevant: the debt forgiven is unpayable and the one refused is trivial.

22.t: Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19, joined. Jesus says everything else hangs on these two.

23.t: Seven denunciations of religious leaders, and then a lament over Jerusalem that shows the anger was grief. Read the last three verses before judging the tone of the first thirty.

24.t: As in Mark, the passage moves between the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the final return. Verse 36 states that the day is unknown even to the Son, which should end all date-setting. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

25.t: The criterion is treatment of the least of these. Whether that means all the poor or Christ's persecuted messengers is debated; either way, professed faith that ignores need is being judged.

Jesus speaks about judgement more often than anyone else in the New Testament, and this verse sets eternal punishment directly beside eternal life, using the same word. The historic Christian view, held across Catholic, Orthodox and nearly all Protestant traditions, is that hell is real and final. A minority of evangelicals, including John Stott, who held the view tentatively, have argued that the lost are ultimately destroyed rather than punished for ever. Both views take judgement seriously. What Scripture is clear on is that judgement is just, that no one will be condemned unfairly, and that Jesus himself came so that no one has to face it. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

26.t: Covenant language from Exodus 24, and the promise not to drink again until the kingdom. Matthew alone adds 'for the forgiveness of sins'.
Jesus stays silent until placed under oath, then answers with Daniel 7 and Psalm 110. The high priest's charge of blasphemy shows what was understood.

27.t: Darkness, the torn curtain, the earthquake, and a Roman officer's confession. Matthew adds tombs opening — a detail unique to him and much discussed.

28.t: All authority, therefore go. The trinitarian formula uses one name for three, and the promise that closes the Gospel answers the name Immanuel that opened it.

12.t: Two Sabbath confrontations. Jesus argues from David eating the consecrated bread and from the priests working on the Sabbath, then claims to be greater than the temple. The claim, not the healing, is what starts the plot in verse 14.

Attributing the Spirit's work to Satan, deliberately and settledly. It describes a hardened position rather than a stray thought, which is why anyone anxious about having committed it has shown by that anxiety that they have not. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
Asked for a sign, Jesus offers only his own death and resurrection. Note that he treats Jonah and the Queen of Sheba as real.

14.t: Matthew alone records Peter getting out of the boat. The rebuke is for doubting rather than for trying, and the chapter ends with the disciples worshipping and calling him the Son of God.

15.t: The Corban abuse again: property dedicated to the temple so that it cannot support ageing parents. Jesus says the heart is what defiles, not the hands.
Her persistence is commended in the strongest terms Matthew gives to anyone's faith, and she is a Gentile.

17.t: Moses and Elijah appear and then vanish, leaving Jesus alone while the Father says to listen to him. Peter's offer to build shelters tries to make permanent what was never meant to be.
A small, strange episode. Jesus argues that sons are exempt, then pays anyway so as not to cause offence — a principle worth more than the coin.

19.t: Jesus goes behind the Mosaic permission to Genesis, treating the creation account as the standard. He grants one exception; the disciples' reaction shows how strict this sounded. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality, and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Beyond those two, Christians differ over whether remarriage is permitted, and churches take genuinely different positions. This is a place to seek counsel from your own church rather than settle it from a note. What is not in doubt is that Jesus treats marriage as a lifelong covenant instituted at creation, and that he says so to people looking for a loophole. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

He asks what good thing he must do, which is already the wrong question. Jesus' answer exposes the idol rather than setting a universal price, and the conclusion — impossible with men, possible with God — is grace stated plainly.

20.t: Those hired last are paid the same. The complaint is fair by every human standard, which is the point: grace is not wages and cannot be audited as though it were.
The mother of James and John asks for the best seats. Jesus answers with the ransom saying — he came to serve and to give his life for many.

21.t: Zechariah 9:9 deliberately enacted, then the temple cleared and the quotation from Isaiah about a house of prayer. Matthew adds that the blind and lame came to him there.
The chief priests understood the parable was about them, which Matthew records. The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is from Psalm 118.

1.t: Luke states his method: eyewitnesses, careful investigation, orderly writing, so that Theophilus may have certainty. The only Gospel to open by explaining itself.
Mary's song is closer to a revolutionary manifesto than a lullaby — the proud scattered, rulers pulled down, the hungry filled. It draws heavily on Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2.

2.t: Luke fixes the birth in datable imperial history. The word often rendered 'inn' more likely means the guest room of a family house.
A disreputable trade, and the first to be told. Luke's interest in the overlooked starts here and never stops.

4.t: Jesus reads Isaiah 61, stops mid-sentence before the day of vengeance, and says it is fulfilled. The crowd turns when he points out that Elijah and Elisha were sent to Gentiles.

5.t: Peter's first reaction to a miracle is to ask Jesus to leave. Luke understands that proximity to holiness is uncomfortable before it is good news.

7.t: Two debtors, two responses, and the point that much forgiveness produces much love. Luke's parallel to this scene is the prodigal son.

10.t: Told to a lawyer trying to limit the definition of neighbour. Jesus reverses the question: not who qualifies, but who acts like one.
Not a rebuke of work but of anxiety. Mary has taken the posture of a disciple, which in that culture was not a woman's place.

15.t: Sheep, coin, son — each with rejoicing at the finding. The elder brother is the point of the third, and the parable is left unfinished because the audience is the elder brother.

16.t: The only parable in which Jesus names one of his own characters. Its sting is the last line: they would not be convinced even if someone rose from the dead.

18.t: The clearest picture of justification in the Gospels. One man lists his record and goes home unjustified; the other asks for mercy and does not.

19.t: Luke's summary of Jesus' mission — to seek and to save the lost — is given at the end of this story rather than the start of the book.

22.t: Jesus tells Peter he has prayed for him and that he will turn back — the failure is predicted and the restoration promised in the same breath.

23.h: Today you will be with me
23.t: Luke alone records the criminal on the cross. Nothing is offered except a request, and nothing is required except it.

24.t: Jesus explains himself from Moses and all the Prophets. The best statement in Scripture of how the Old Testament is to be read.
He eats fish to prove he is not a ghost. Luke insists on the physicality of the resurrection.

3.t: Luke fixes John's ministry against six named rulers. He is writing history and wants it checkable.
Where Matthew traces Jesus to Abraham, Luke goes to Adam and then to God. His Gospel is for everyone, not only for Israel.

6.t: Luke's version is blunter than Matthew's: blessed are you who are poor, and woe to you who are rich. He does not spiritualise it.
The hardest instruction in the Gospels, grounded not in results but in the character of the Father who is kind to the ungrateful.

8.t: Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, and says they supported the work out of their own means. No other Gospel records this.
Two demonstrations of authority, over nature and over the demonic. The healed man is told to stay and tell, which is the opposite of the usual instruction.

9.h: Who do you say I am
9.t: Luke places Peter's confession after a note that Jesus was praying alone. The call to take up the cross follows immediately, with Luke's addition: daily.
The turn of the Gospel. From here everything moves toward Jerusalem, and when a Samaritan village refuses him, he rebukes the disciples rather than the village.

11.t: Luke's shorter form of the Lord's Prayer, followed by the friend at midnight and the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Persistence is commended, not because God is reluctant but because we are.
Luke's version of the denunciations, delivered over dinner at a Pharisee's house. The charge against the lawyers is that they took away the key of knowledge.

12.t: A man with a good harvest and no thought beyond himself. God's verdict lands on the one thing he had not planned for.
The ravens and the lilies again, ending with the instruction to sell possessions and give — Luke is consistently more concrete about money than Matthew.

13.t: Two disasters, and Jesus refuses the assumption that the victims were worse sinners. He turns the question back on the askers.
Asked whether few will be saved, Jesus does not answer the arithmetic. He tells them to strive to enter.

14.t: Table etiquette as kingdom instruction, ending with the advice to invite those who cannot repay.
The tower builder and the king going to war. Jesus is actively thinning a crowd here, which is worth noticing.

17.t: Ten lepers healed, one returns, and he is a Samaritan. Luke's interest in the outsider surfaces again.
Not coming with observable signs. The phrase can be rendered 'within you' or 'among you'; the second fits the context, since he is speaking to Pharisees.

20.t: As in Matthew and Mark. Luke notes the people's reaction — may it never be — which shows they understood.
Jesus poses the puzzle from Psalm 110 and leaves it hanging. The answer is the incarnation.

21.t: Luke places this immediately before the temple's destruction is predicted, as Mark does. She gives everything to something about to fall.
Luke's version is more explicit than Mark's about armies surrounding Jerusalem, which many take as evidence of how the AD 70 element was understood.

1.t: Factions named after leaders — and Paul's response is to be glad he baptised almost nobody, which tells you how seriously he took the personality cult.
The cross as scandal to Jews and nonsense to Greeks. God chose the weak and the low to nullify the things that are, so that nobody boasts before him.

2.t: Paul compares the Spirit to a person's own spirit, knowing what is within — and says we have the mind of Christ. A key passage on how Scripture is understood.

3.t: Work tested by fire; some survives, some burns, and the builder is saved either way. The passage is about ministry, not salvation.

5.t: A case of incest the congregation is proud of tolerating. Paul's instruction is severe, and 2 Corinthians 2 shows it was aimed at restoration. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

6.t: A list of those who will not inherit the kingdom, followed immediately by the past tense. The verse is quoted far more often for its first half than its second.

7.t: Paul answers questions they sent. He treats singleness as a genuine good rather than a waiting room, which was unusual then and is unusual now.

9.t: Adaptation in method, never in message — Paul says this within a chapter about surrendering rights.

10.t: Two promises: it is common, and there is a way out. Neither says the pressure will be removed.

11.h: The Supper, received and handed on
11.t: The earliest written account of the Lord's Supper, predating the Gospels. Paul says he received it from the Lord.

Christians have divided over this for five hundred years. Roman Catholics hold the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; Lutherans that he is present in and with them; the Reformed that he is truly present to faith by the Spirit though the elements do not change; and many evangelicals that it is chiefly a memorial. We stand with the Reformed view, and we would not refuse the table to a brother holding any of the others. What nobody disputes is that Jesus commanded it and that it proclaims his death until he comes. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

12.t: Gifts differ, the Spirit does not. Verse 11 says the Spirit distributes to each one as he wills, which is a statement about a person rather than a power.

This is a live disagreement among evangelicals and within Reformed churches. Cessationists hold that the revelatory and sign gifts ceased with the apostles; continuationists that the Spirit still gives them, while insisting everything be tested by Scripture. Both are held by serious people. What Paul actually argues in this chapter is not about timing at all: the gifts differ, the Spirit does not, and they exist for the common good rather than for display. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

13.t: Written as a correction to a congregation obsessed with the spectacular, not as a wedding reading. Its position between two chapters on gifts is the argument.

15.t: Verses 3 to 5 are a formula Paul received and passed on, dating within a few years of the crucifixion. It is the single most important piece of evidence for the early belief in the resurrection.

15.h: If Christ has not been raised
15.t: Paul stakes everything on a historical claim and says that if it is false, Christians are to be pitied. He does not offer a fallback.
Not a ghost and not the same body unchanged — sown perishable, raised imperishable. The chapter ends in the only place it could: therefore stand firm.

16.t: An Aramaic prayer — our Lord, come — preserved in a Greek letter. Evidence that the earliest Aramaic-speaking Christians prayed directly to Jesus.

4.t: Paul refuses to be judged by the Corinthians, and then says he does not even judge himself. The verdict that matters comes later and from elsewhere.
Heavy irony. Paul contrasts their self-satisfaction with the apostles' actual conditions: hungry, beaten, homeless, treated as the world's rubbish.

8.t: On food offered to idols. Paul agrees with the strong on the facts and then subordinates the point to love for the weaker brother.
Paul takes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 and distributes its two terms — God and Lord — between the Father and Jesus, inside an argument for monotheism.

14.t: Paul's consistent criterion is whether the church is built up. Five intelligible words are worth more than ten thousand nobody understands.

Everything in a fitting and orderly way, because God is not a God of disorder. The passage on women speaking is among the most disputed in Paul, and the honest position is that its scope is contested. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

14.h: The hardest verses in the chapter
14.t: Paul's instruction about women being silent is genuinely difficult, partly because he has already assumed in chapter 11 that women pray and prophesy in the gathering. Readings include a restriction on judging prophecy, on disruptive questioning, or on the authoritative teaching office. Anyone who tells you this is simple has not read it carefully. Whatever its scope, it sits inside a chapter whose stated aim is order and the building up of the church. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: Comfort received becomes comfort given. Paul then says he despaired of life itself, which is not the language of a man performing strength.

4.t: Cheap pottery, so that the power is evidently God's. The metaphor governs the whole letter.
Both at once, daily. Paul does not deny the decline; he sets it against what is unseen.

5.t: Not a improved version but a new act of creation, with the old gone.
He who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. As compressed a statement of substitution as exists.

8.t: An argument for generosity that runs entirely through the incarnation.

12.t: Three requests, refused, with an answer better than the request. Paul asked the Lord directly and received a reply — with no vision in view.
Power perfected in weakness. Paul's conclusion is not resignation but boasting in the very thing he asked to be rid of.

2.t: Paul urges forgiveness for the man disciplined in the first letter, so that he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Discipline aimed at restoration, and here completed.

3.t: A contrast between a ministry carved on stone and one written by the Spirit on hearts. It ends with transformation from glory to glory.

6.t: A list of hardships offered as evidence of ministry: beatings, imprisonments, sleepless nights. Sorrowful yet always rejoicing, having nothing yet possessing everything.

7.t: Godly grief produces repentance without regret; worldly grief produces death. A distinction worth holding onto.

9.t: Sow sparingly, reap sparingly. Paul is raising a collection for Jerusalem and refuses to pressure them into it.

10.t: Demolishing arguments and taking every thought captive. Often quoted for spiritual warfare generally; the immediate context is a dispute over Paul's authority.

11.t: Paul lists his sufferings only under protest, and ends with the escape from Damascus in a basket — a deliberately undignified climax.

13.t: A direct instruction to test whether you are in the faith, which sits oddly with assumptions that such examination is morbid.
The closing benediction names Father, Son and Spirit in one sentence, and is still said in churches every week.

4.t: Written to a church grieving and confused about whether Christians who died would miss the return. Paul's aim is stated: so that you may not grieve as others do — not that you may not grieve.

5.t: Three short commands, described as God's will. Note 'in all circumstances', not 'for'.

1.t: Not in word only but in power and in the Holy Spirit. Paul's evidence for their election is the change in how they live.

2.t: Paul describes his ministry among them as gentle, and then as a father encouraging his children. He also says he worked night and day so as not to burden them.

3.t: Paul could not bear not knowing how they were. The letter is unusually affectionate throughout.

2.t: Among the most disputed passages in Paul. The restrainer has been identified as Rome, the gospel, the Spirit and more. Paul assumes his readers know; we do not. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

3.h: If a man will not work
3.t: Aimed at those who had stopped working because they thought the day had come, not at people unable to find work.

1.t: God is just, and will repay. Paul offers a persecuted church the comfort of a final reckoning rather than a promise that the pressure will stop.
Paul's self-description, in the present tense, decades after his conversion.

2.t: One God, one mediator, one ransom for all. A compact statement that excludes any other route.

2.h: Men and women in the church
2.t: This passage is the centre of a long and honest disagreement among evangelicals. Complementarians read it as restricting the teaching and governing office of the church to qualified men, on the basis of the creation order Paul cites. Egalitarians read it as addressing a specific disorder in Ephesus. Reformed churches are overwhelmingly complementarian and that is where this group stands; we also recognise that the other position is held by people who love Scripture. Note what the passage does not say: nothing here concerns a woman's worth, ability or standing before God. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

3.t: The qualifications are almost entirely about character rather than ability. Only one — able to teach — concerns competence. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

3.h: Elders, and what the qualifications are for
3.t: Almost every item is about character rather than gifting, and the office is plural throughout the New Testament — a church has elders, not an elder. 'Husband of one wife' is most likely a call to marital faithfulness rather than a rule excluding single or widowed men, though churches read it differently. A man's home is treated as evidence of how he would handle a congregation. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

6.t: The love of money, not money, is the root. Verse 6 is the positive form of the same point.

4.t: Physical training has some value; godliness has value for everything. The verb is the one behind our word gymnasium.

4.h: Let no one despise your youth
4.t: Timothy was probably in his thirties. The answer to being underestimated is to be exemplary rather than assertive.

5.t: Detailed instruction on who the church should support. The principle underneath — families first, the church for those with nobody — is still sound.
A single practical aside about Timothy's stomach, preserved in Scripture. A useful corrective to over-spiritualising every verse.

2.t: A trustworthy saying that ends on God's faithfulness to himself rather than on our performance.

3.t: The classic text on inspiration. Note what it is said to equip for — every good work, not merely correct belief.

4.t: In season and out. Paul's last charge, written expecting execution.
The most personal paragraph Paul wrote. He asks for his cloak and his scrolls, names those who deserted him, and asks that it not be held against them.

1.t: Timothy's faith is traced to his grandmother and mother. The clearest New Testament picture of faith passed down a family.
But of power, love and self-discipline. Written to a man who evidently needed telling.

2.t: Grace is described as a teacher, which prevents any reading that sets it against holiness.

3.t: Washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, justified by his grace. Salvation presented as trinitarian throughout.

1.t: The qualifications match 1 Timothy 3 closely and are overwhelmingly about character. The one competence required is holding firmly to sound teaching so as to encourage and refute.

Paul says explicitly that he could order Philemon and chooses to appeal instead. He offers to pay the debt himself, and asks him to receive Onesimus as a brother — which quietly makes the institution untenable.
The opening sentence is among the finest Greek in the New Testament. The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of his being, and he sustains all things.
A chain of seven Old Testament quotations. At verse 8 the Son is addressed as God, and at verse 10 a psalm addressed to the LORD is applied to him as creator.

2.t: He took flesh and blood in order to die, and to become a merciful and faithful high priest. The reason given for the incarnation is the cross.

3.t: The writer introduces Psalm 95 as the Spirit speaking, and what follows is God in the first person — the same move made at 10:15.

4.t: The word as a sword dividing to the joints and marrow. Nothing is hidden from the one to whom we must give account.
A high priest who has been tempted in every way and did not sin. The throne of grace is approached boldly precisely because of who stands beside it.

6.t: The hardest paragraph in Hebrews. Readings divide between genuine apostasy, hypothetical warning, and professing but unregenerate people. Note that the writer immediately says he is confident of better things concerning them. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

Read the warning of verses 4 to 8 with this verse attached, because the writer attaches it himself. Our position is the historic Reformed one, set out in the Westminster Confession 17.1: those whom God has accepted can neither totally nor finally fall away, and the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep them. The Remonstrant tradition, following Arminius, holds the opposite. Others read the passage as describing believers who can genuinely be lost. Either way the warning is meant to be felt rather than explained away. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
The image behind this group's own emblem. The anchor holds because it is fixed inside the sanctuary where Jesus has gone ahead.

7.t: He always lives to intercede. The argument is that a priest who does not die needs no successor and makes no repeat sacrifice.

9.t: The repeated point of the letter. A single sacrifice, not repeated, entering the real sanctuary rather than its copy.

10.t: Jeremiah 31 introduced as the Holy Spirit speaking — and inside the quotation, the speaker is identified as the LORD.

10.h: The passage this group takes its name from
10.t: Hold fast the confession, consider one another to provoke love and good works, do not neglect meeting together, encourage one another. Three commands, all corporate.

As with chapter 6, the language is severe and the writer immediately follows it in verse 39 by saying they are not those who shrink back. Take the warning seriously and take the assurance seriously; the letter gives you both and does not treat them as a contradiction. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

11.t: Faith defined and then illustrated. Note the turn at verse 35: some were delivered and some were tortured, and both are listed as faith.

12.t: The image is an arena with the previous chapter's witnesses in the stands. Fix your eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter.
Painful at the time, yielding a harvest afterwards, and evidence of sonship rather than rejection.

13.h: The same yesterday, today and forever
13.t: Placed among practical instructions rather than in a doctrinal section, which is where its comfort actually lands.

5.t: A glimpse of Gethsemane from outside the Gospels. He learned obedience from what he suffered, which does not mean he moved from disobedience but that he experienced what obeying costs.
The writer breaks off to rebuke them for needing milk. It sets up the warning of chapter 6.

8.t: The argument turns on Jeremiah 31, quoted at length. Calling the first covenant obsolete was a startling thing to write to Jewish believers.

1.t: The Greek construction here matches four others in this short letter that are rendered of one person. Worth comparing 1:11, 2:20, 3:2 and 3:18.
Peter appeals to what he saw at the transfiguration, then says the prophetic word is more certain still. Verse 21 on how Scripture came about is foundational.

3.t: The delay is patience, not absence. A day is as a thousand years — a statement about God's relation to time, used pastorally.

2.t: A fierce chapter, parallel to Jude. The marks given are exploitation, sensuality and greed — conduct rather than only doctrine.

1.t: A short letter about not supporting travelling teachers who deny the incarnation. Written when hospitality meant funding a mission.
A man who loves to be first and puts people out of the church. John names him, which is unusual and instructive.
Once for all delivered — the faith is not open to revision, which is the premise of the whole letter.
Jude cites a book outside the canon. That he quotes it does not make the book Scripture, any more than Paul quoting Greek poets canonises them.
One of the great doxologies. Able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless — the letter ends on God's work, not ours.
The word means unveiling. A blessing is pronounced on the one who reads it aloud and those who hear — it was written to be read in church.
John describes him with Daniel's phrase for the son of man, and then with Daniel's description of the Ancient of Days. Note the titles at verse 17: the First and the Last.

2.t: Real churches with specific problems. The pattern is consistent: what he knows, what is wrong, what to do, and a promise to the one who conquers.

3.t: Lukewarm, in a city with a famously tepid water supply. The image is not half-hearted versus zealous but useless versus useful. He stands at the door and knocks — addressed to a church, not to unbelievers.

4.t: Before any judgement, a throne room. The structure matters: whatever follows, this is the fixed point.

5.t: John hears of a Lion and turns to see a slain Lamb. The reversal is the theological centre of the book. Every creature then worships the one on the throne and the Lamb together.

6.t: Conquest, war, famine, death — and under the altar, the question 'how long'. Revelation does not pretend that history is comfortable. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

7.t: From every nation, tribe, people and language — the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham. God will wipe away every tear.

12.t: A retelling of the whole conflict in symbol. The dragon is identified plainly at verse 9, and he is defeated by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.

13.t: Political and religious power in league. The number is most persuasively read as a coded reference to Nero, whose name in Hebrew letters totals 666, though other readings exist. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

19.h: The rider on the white horse
19.t: The return, in warfare imagery — but note that his robe is dipped in blood before the battle begins, and the weapon is a sword from his mouth.

20.t: The passage that divides millennial views. Amillennial, premillennial and postmillennial readings have all been held by serious Christians. Our group does not make it a test of fellowship. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

20.h: How to hold a passage like this
20.t: Christians who agree on everything else divide over the thousand years, and have since the early centuries. Amillennialists read it as the present age between the cross and the return; postmillennialists as a coming era of gospel success; premillennialists as a literal reign after Christ returns. Each can point to real evidence. What all three hold is what the chapter is actually for: Christ reigns, his people are secure, and evil is finally and completely dealt with. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

21.t: Not escape from creation but its renewal. The dwelling of God is with man — the sentence Eden lost and the whole Bible has been moving back toward.
Because God and the Lamb are its temple. The whole sacrificial system ends by becoming unnecessary.

22.t: One voice claims to be the Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, and four verses later identifies itself: I, Jesus, sent my angel. No change of speaker is marked between.
The Spirit and the bride say it, and then anyone who wishes may take the water of life freely. The Bible ends with an invitation.

8.t: Half an hour of it, before the trumpets. The prayers of the saints go up with the incense — they are part of what sets the sequence in motion.

9.t: Locusts and horsemen, drawing on Joel. The chapter ends noting that the survivors still did not repent, which is its actual point.

10.t: John eats it and finds it sweet then bitter, as Ezekiel did. Speaking God's word is both of those things.

11.t: Drawing on Moses, Elijah and Zechariah 4. Identifications vary widely; the pattern — testimony, apparent defeat, vindication — does not.
The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord. Handel set these words, and the tense is decisive: it is announced as already done.

14.t: A deliberate counterpoint to the beast of chapter 13. The 144,000 are marked on the forehead as the beast's followers are.
Proclaimed to every nation, tribe, language and people — even here, judgement and invitation run together.

15.h: The song of Moses and of the Lamb
15.t: Exodus imagery: those who have come through the sea stand beside it and sing. The last plagues follow.

16.t: The final sequence, echoing the plagues on Egypt. Verse 15 interrupts with a beatitude on the one who stays awake — the pastoral aim showing through the symbolism.

17.t: A city on seven hills, drunk on the blood of the saints, which first-century readers would have read as Rome. The name stands for every power that sets itself against God.

18.t: A dirge sung by kings, merchants and sailors, all of whom mourn the loss of trade rather than of people. Verse 13 ends the cargo list with human beings.

3.t: The bush burns without being consumed. God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — by relationship before by attribute.
The name given is deliberately open: I am who I am. Jesus' 'before Abraham was, I am' reaches back here.

6.t: God's answer to Moses' complaint is a chain of first-person promises. Redemption is entirely his initiative.

12.t: The lamb without defect, the blood on the doorposts, the judgement passing over. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb; John notes that no bone of his was broken.
Without defect, blood on the doorframes, the meal eaten ready to travel. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb.

14.t: Stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. Israel contributes nothing to the rescue except walking through it.

19.t: The identity given to Israel at Sinai, and the words Peter applies to the church.
The people are warned not to touch the mountain. Hebrews 12 contrasts this scene with the one believers have come to.

20.t: Note the preface: I am the LORD your God who brought you out of Egypt. The law follows the rescue rather than earning it.
The people ask Moses to speak instead. Fear of God is right; this is what it looks like when it goes wrong.

32.t: Six weeks after Sinai. Aaron's account of how it happened is one of the feeblest excuses in Scripture.
Moses offers himself in their place. Paul says something similar about Israel in Romans 9.

33.h: I will not go with you
33.t: God offers the land without his presence. Moses refuses the offer, which is the right answer and not an obvious one.
God passes by and proclaims his own name. Mark uses this 'passing by' language of Jesus on the water.

40.t: The book ends with God moving in. Everything Exodus has been building toward is this.

4.t: Moses objects repeatedly and God answers each one, until the LORD's anger burns and Aaron is appointed. Reluctance is met patiently and then firmly.

7.t: The stated purpose throughout is that Egypt will know that he is the LORD. Each plague is aimed at a god the Egyptians worshipped.

15.t: Israel's oldest poem. Miriam leads the women with tambourines. Revelation 15 calls the final song the song of Moses.

16.t: Enough for the day, and it rots if hoarded. Jesus draws on this in John 6, and the Lord's Prayer asks for daily bread.

17.t: Paul says the rock was Christ. Note that God stands on the rock and tells Moses to strike it — the blow falls where God is.
Aaron and Hur support Moses' arms until sunset. A picture of what holding one another up actually looks like.

24.t: Half the blood on the altar, half on the people. Jesus takes this exact phrase at the Last Supper. Then the elders see God and eat.

34.t: Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness — and by no means clearing the guilty. The most quoted self-description of God in the Old Testament.

1.h: A king who did not know Joseph
1.t: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah defy him and are named in Scripture, while the Pharaoh is not.

2.h: Forty years on the back of a desert
2.t: Moses' attempt to deliver Israel by his own hand fails completely. God hears, remembers, sees and knows — four verbs that set up everything after.

5.t: The first result of obedience is heavier work and the people turning on Moses. He takes the complaint straight to God.

13.t: God deliberately avoids the short road so they will not face war and turn back. Guidance is not always the direct route.

8.t: From the third plague the magicians cannot copy it and admit it is the finger of God. Pharaoh's hardening is described both as his own doing and as God's — Scripture holds both without resolving them. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

9.t: A distinction is now made between Egypt and Israel. Some of Pharaoh's officials fear the word of the LORD and bring their animals in — faith appearing even in Egypt.

Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it, and the sequence matters. God announces in advance, before any plague, that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21, 7:3); through the first five plagues the text describes Pharaoh hardening his own; from 9:12 it says the LORD hardened it. The historic Reformed reading is that God's announced purpose and Pharaoh's real choices are both true, and that God gave him over to a resistance he had already chosen — confirming a hard heart rather than corrupting a willing one. Others hold that God's hardening is judicial withdrawal, letting Pharaoh have his way. Paul takes up the episode in Romans 9 to show God's freedom in mercy, and answers the objection it raises rather than removing it. Scripture holds sovereignty and responsibility together without resolving the tension, and so should we. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

10.t: Pharaoh's negotiations narrow each time: go, but not far; go, but leave the children; go, but leave the flocks. The demand from God never shrinks.
