11.t: The death of the firstborn, the gravest thing in the book and the hardest to read. It answers Pharaoh's own slaughter of Hebrew boys in chapter 1, and Israel's firstborn are spared only by the blood. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

18.t: Moses is judging the people from morning to evening, and his father-in-law tells him plainly it will wear him out. The origin of delegated leadership, taken from a Midianite priest.

21.t: Case law for an ancient society, including rules on slavery that regulate an existing institution rather than approve it. 'Eye for eye' was a limit on revenge, not a licence for it. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

21.h: Does the Bible approve of slavery
21.t: The honest answer is that the law regulated an institution that existed everywhere in the ancient world rather than abolishing it, as Jesus said of divorce, because of hardness of heart. The hardest texts must be faced first. Leviticus 25:44–46 permits buying foreign slaves as inheritable property for life, on different terms from Hebrew servants who went free after six years. Exodus 21:20–21 penalises a master who kills a slave outright but not one whose slave survives a day or two, adding the chilling reason that the slave is his property. Christians should not explain these away. Alongside them stand provisions unlike anything in surrounding law codes: kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (21:16), an injured slave went free (21:26–27), and a runaway was not to be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15). The New Testament never commands slavery and plants principles that undid it — every person made in God's image, no slave or free in Christ, Philemon receiving Onesimus as a brother — which Wilberforce and the abolitionists drew on directly. Christians have answered the remaining difficulty in different ways: that God accommodated law to a hard society while pointing beyond it, or that these regulations limited an evil he did not yet abolish. Neither answer makes the texts comfortable. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

22.h: The widow, the orphan and the foreigner
22.t: God says he will hear their cry himself. The concern for the vulnerable is built into the law code from its first pages.

23.t: Do not follow the crowd in doing wrong, do not favour the poor or the rich in a lawsuit, do not take a bribe. Remarkably modern in its demands.

25.t: Seven chapters of design. The point is stated in verse 8: make a sanctuary so I may dwell among them. Hebrews reads the whole structure as a copy of the heavenly reality.

26.t: The curtain separating the Most Holy Place is the one torn from top to bottom at the crucifixion.

27.t: Placed first as you entered — nobody approaches God without passing sacrifice.

28.t: He carries the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart. Hebrews presents Jesus as the priest who carries his people in the same way.

29.t: Seven days of consecration, ending with the promise that God will dwell among them and be their God — the covenant formula repeated through the whole Bible.

30.t: The atonement money is the same for rich and poor: every life costs the same to redeem.

31.t: The first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and it is for craftsmanship. Skilled work is presented as a spiritual gift.

35.t: The materials come as freewill offerings, from men and women alike. Chapter 36 records that they had to be told to stop giving.

36.t: The only recorded occasion in Scripture where people were restrained from giving.

37.h: The ark and the mercy seat
37.t: The lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Paul uses the same word for Christ in Romans 3:25.

38.t: An exact reckoning of the metals used. Public accountability for money given to God, recorded in Scripture.

39.t: Said repeatedly. Moses inspects the work and blesses the people — obedience and blessing together.

1.t: Wholly consumed, nothing kept back. The sacrificial system opens with total surrender rather than with sin.

16.t: Two goats: one killed, one driven out bearing the sins. Together they picture what Hebrews says one sacrifice accomplished.

17.h: The life is in the blood
17.t: The verse explaining the entire sacrificial logic, and the one Hebrews builds on.

19.h: Leave the edges of your field
19.t: For the poor and the foreigner. The chapter mixes worship, wages, justice and neighbour-love without separating them.
Buried in a chapter of miscellaneous law, and named by Jesus as second only to loving God.

10.t: Nadab and Abihu die at the altar. A hard chapter about the seriousness of approaching God on your own terms. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

11.t: Dietary law as a daily reminder of separation. Mark 7:19 records that Jesus declared all foods clean.

18.h: Do not live as they do
18.t: Sexual law framed as the difference between Israel and the nations around it, and grounded in the repeated refrain: I am the LORD.

23.t: Sabbath, Passover, Firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, Atonement, Tabernacles. The calendar itself teaches the story.

25.t: Every fiftieth year, debts cancelled and land returned. Whether Israel ever kept it is doubtful; the principle behind it is not.

26.t: The covenant sanctions, ending with a promise to remember the covenant even in exile.

4.t: Still requiring a sacrifice. The category itself teaches that guilt is not only about intention.

6.h: The fire must not go out
6.t: Kept burning continuously on the altar. A small instruction that has preached well for centuries.

8.t: Seven days of it, with blood applied to the ear, thumb and toe — hearing, doing and walking all consecrated.

20.h: You are to be holy to me
20.t: Because I am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations. The stated reason for the whole code.

2.t: Flour, oil and salt — no yeast or honey. An offering of daily bread, acknowledging that the harvest was God's.

3.t: Shared: part burned, part eaten by the priests, part by the worshipper. A meal in God's presence, the forerunner of the Lord's Supper.

5.t: If a person cannot afford a lamb, two birds; if not birds, a little flour. No one is priced out of atonement.

7.t: The thanksgiving offering had to be eaten promptly. Thanks was to be expressed, not stored.

9.t: Aaron's first sacrifice is consumed by fire from the LORD and the people shout and fall face down. Worship accepted, visibly.

12.t: Ritual uncleanness, not moral guilt. Mary's offering of two birds in Luke 2 shows the family were poor.

13.t: The Hebrew term covers several conditions, not modern leprosy specifically. The priest's role was diagnostic, and exclusion from the camp was isolation rather than punishment.

14.t: The ritual for restoration after healing. Jesus sends the healed leper to show himself to the priest, following this chapter.

15.t: Ritual rules touching intimate life. They taught that God's holiness reached every part of existence. The woman who touched Jesus' cloak was under these laws.

21.t: Stricter than for others, because they stood closer. Physical defects barred a priest from serving at the altar, which Christians read as pointing to the need for a perfect high priest rather than as a verdict on disabled people. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

22.t: No blemished animal. Malachi's rebuke — offering the lame and the sick — is aimed straight at this chapter.

24.t: A grim case, and one where the law applies equally to the foreigner and the native-born. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

27.t: Rules for what is promised to God and how it can be redeemed. Leviticus ends not with sacrifice but with the seriousness of what people say they will give.

6.t: Voluntary, temporary, and marked by abstaining from wine and leaving the hair uncut. Samson and Samuel were both under it from birth.
The Aaronic blessing, still used weekly in churches. The oldest known fragment of biblical text is a silver amulet carrying it.

13.t: Ten spies report giants, two report God. The nation believes the ten and spends forty years in consequence.
In our own eyes, and we looked the same to them. The report is accurate about the giants and wrong about God.

11.t: Moses asks God whether he conceived this people. The Spirit is put on seventy elders, and Moses wishes all the LORD's people were prophets.

12.t: They challenge Moses over his Cushite wife and over his standing. Moses, described as the most humble man on earth, prays for Miriam's healing.

14.t: They say it would be better to die in Egypt, and God takes them at their word. Caleb and Joshua alone of that generation enter.

16.t: A challenge to Moses' and Aaron's authority that ends in the ground opening. Jude 11 uses it as a warning. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

20.t: Moses is told to speak to it and hits it twice. The cost is that he does not enter the land — which reads as severe until you notice what he claimed in verse 10.

22.t: A pagan seer hired to curse Israel, and a donkey with better spiritual sight than its owner. 2 Peter and Jude both use him as a picture of teaching for money.

1.t: A fighting force counted at Sinai. The book's English name comes from this; the Hebrew name is 'In the wilderness', which fits it better.

3.h: The Levites instead of the firstborn
3.t: Taken in place of every firstborn son God claimed at the Passover. Substitution built into the structure of Israel's worship.

9.t: They moved when it lifted and stayed when it settled, however long that was. Guidance as obedience to something you do not control.

10.t: Moses asks his brother-in-law to come with them, despite the cloud. Divine guidance and local knowledge are not treated as rivals.

15.t: A visible reminder on the edge of the garment so they would remember the commands. The woman with the bleeding touched the edge of Jesus' cloak.

21.t: Looking at the image of the thing killing them brings life. Jesus applies it to himself in John 3:14.

23.h: God is not a man, that he should lie
23.t: Spoken by Balaam, of all people, and one of the clearest statements of God's constancy in Scripture.

27.t: Five women petition for an inheritance and the law is changed in their favour. Moses takes the case to God rather than dismissing it.

32.h: The two and a half tribes
32.t: They want land east of the Jordan and are made to fight for their brothers first. Settling early is permitted; leaving others to fight is not.

35.t: Six towns where someone who killed accidentally could flee the avenger. Ancient law distinguishing manslaughter from murder.

2.t: Every tribe in position, with God's dwelling at the centre. The layout itself is theology.

4.t: The Kohathites carry the sacred objects but may not look at them. The Uzzah incident in 2 Samuel 6 turns on exactly this.

5.h: The test for a suspected wife
5.t: An ordeal ritual that troubles modern readers. In its setting it removed the matter from the husband's hands and placed it before God, which was a protection as well as a test. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

7.t: The longest chapter in the Pentateuch, repeating the same gift twelve times. Every tribe's gift is recorded in full, as if each mattered individually.

8.t: Given to Aaron as a gift from the people. Their service begins at twenty-five and ends at fifty.

17.t: It buds, blossoms and produces almonds overnight — God settling a dispute about leadership with something only he could do.

18.t: The Levites receive no land. God himself is their inheritance, and the tithe supports them.

19.t: A cleansing ritual for contact with death. Hebrews 9 contrasts its outward cleansing with Christ's cleansing of the conscience.

24.t: Balaam, hired to curse, prophesies a king. Early Jewish and Christian readers alike took it as messianic.

25.t: Where Balaam's curses failed, his advice succeeded: seduction into idolatry. Revelation 2 names Balaam's teaching as the cause.

26.t: A new generation counted. Not one of the first census remained except Caleb and Joshua.

28.t: Every morning and every evening, without exception. Worship built into the rhythm of every day.

29.t: Trumpets, Atonement and Tabernacles, with their offerings. The number of bulls at Tabernacles decreases daily from thirteen to seven.

30.t: A woman's vow could be annulled by her father or husband on the day he heard it. The law assumes household responsibility; the principle for everyone is to keep your word.

31.t: One of the most difficult chapters in Scripture, and it should not be read quickly or explained away. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

33.t: A list of forty-two stages from Egypt to the Jordan. The journey is remembered stop by stop.

34.t: The land described precisely. The promise to Abraham becomes a map.

36.t: The book ends by protecting the inheritance of five women. Numbers closes on a small detail of justice.

6.t: Israel's core confession: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Jesus names the command that follows as the greatest.
The answer commanded is a story: we were slaves in Egypt and the LORD brought us out. Catechism by narrative.

8.t: The danger addressed is not famine but prosperity — that when you are full you will forget who fed you.

8.h: Man does not live on bread alone
8.t: Quoted by Jesus in the wilderness. The forty years are described as humbling and testing to reveal what was in their hearts.

18.h: Do not learn their detestable ways
18.t: Divination, mediums, consulting the dead. The alternative offered is a prophet, in the next verse.
The promise Peter applies to Jesus in Acts 3, and in the same passage the test for a false prophet: if what he says does not happen, the LORD did not speak it.

30.h: The LORD will circumcise your hearts
30.t: So that you may love him. Deuteronomy itself admits the law cannot produce what it requires.
The covenant set out as a decision with consequences. Paul picks up verses 12 to 14 in Romans 10.

34.t: He sees the land and does not enter. The book ends saying no prophet like him has since arisen — which is what makes 18:15 a promise still open.

10.t: Fear him, walk in his ways, love him, serve him. Then, startlingly, that he loves the foreigner and so should they.

29.t: Belong to the LORD; the things revealed belong to us and our children. A short verse that settles a great deal of speculation.

4.t: So that you do not forget, and so that you teach your children. Almost every exhortation in Deuteronomy runs on memory.

7.h: Why did God command the destruction of the Canaanites
7.t: This is the most serious moral objection raised against the Old Testament, and the honest starting point is what the texts actually say: the commands include women and children (Deuteronomy 20:16–18, 1 Samuel 15:3), and no Christian should pretend otherwise. Several things are true alongside that. The judgement falls on specific nations for specific practices, including child sacrifice, and Genesis 15:16 says it was delayed four hundred years until their sin reached its full measure. It is limited to one time and place and never given as a pattern for anyone since. God applied the same standard to Israel, sending them into exile for the same sins, and Rahab and her family were spared when she turned to him. Many scholars also argue that ancient war reports used deliberately sweeping language — 'left no survivors' — since the same peoples reappear shortly afterwards in the same books; others find that argument insufficient, and it does not by itself remove the commands. Christians have responded by seeing this as God's unique judicial act as judge of all the earth, by reading the conquest as a limited episode within a larger story, or by admitting they cannot fully reconcile it and holding it alongside the character of God shown at the cross. That last answer is more honest than a tidy one. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.
God's choice is traced to his love and his oath rather than to anything in them. Election stated plainly in the Old Testament.

9.t: Said three times in three verses, as if Moses expected them to miss it.

11.t: On your hands, on your foreheads, on your doorframes, talked about at home and on the road. Faith passed on by repetition rather than by event.

31.t: Said to the nation, then to Joshua, and picked up in Hebrews 13 and applied to the reader.

32.t: A national anthem of warning, to be memorised so that it testifies against them later. Verse 4 — the Rock, all his ways are just — is the best known line.

17.t: He must not accumulate horses, wives or silver, and must write out a copy of the law for himself. Solomon breaks all four.

28.t: Fourteen verses of blessing and fifty-four of curse. The imbalance is deliberate and the detail is harrowing.

1.t: It takes eleven days from Horeb to the border. It took them forty years. The book opens with that arithmetic.

2.t: Israel is told not to provoke Edom, Moab or Ammon, because God has given them their land too. God's care is not confined to Israel.

3.t: He asks and is told: enough, do not speak to me again about this. Unanswered prayer from the greatest prophet of the Old Testament.

5.t: The Sabbath reason changes from creation (Exodus 20) to rescue from Egypt. Rest is grounded in grace as well as in creation.

12.t: One sanctuary rather than many shrines. Worship is to be on God's terms, not wherever is convenient.

13.h: A prophet whose sign comes true
13.t: If he leads you after other gods, do not listen. Accurate predictions do not validate a teacher; faithfulness to God does.

14.t: Eaten in joy before the LORD, and every third year given to the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow.

15.t: Every seventh year. Verse 11 — there will always be poor people — is followed by the command to be openhanded toward them, not by resignation.

16.t: Appoint judges who will not pervert justice or take bribes. The Hebrew repeats the word for emphasis.

19.t: A system distinguishing accidental killing from murder, and protecting the innocent from revenge.

20.t: Including exemptions for the newly married, the fearful, and those who have just planted a vineyard. And do not cut down fruit trees during a siege.

21.h: Cursed is anyone hung on a tree
21.t: Paul quotes it in Galatians 3: Christ became a curse for us.

22.t: You may not ignore a stray animal. Care for a neighbour's property is written into law.

23.h: Do not return a runaway slave
23.t: A remarkable law among ancient codes, which generally required the opposite.

24.t: The text Jesus says was given because of hardness of heart. It limited abuse rather than endorsing divorce. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

25.t: Paul applies it twice to paying those who teach.

26.t: A wandering Aramean was my father — the worshipper recites the whole story when bringing the harvest.

27.t: Twelve curses, with the people answering Amen to each. Covenant accepted publicly.

33.h: The eternal God is your refuge
33.t: And underneath are the everlasting arms. Moses' final blessing.

1.t: The book opens by naming the loss and then moving on. Joshua's commission is threefold: be strong, be courageous, obey the book.
Repeated three times, and tied each time to obedience and to the book of the law rather than to confidence.

2.t: A Canaanite prostitute who hides the spies because she has heard what God did at the sea. She appears in Matthew's genealogy and in Hebrews 11.

24.t: Joshua rehearses it from Abraham onward before asking for a decision. He argues from history rather than from sentiment.
Joshua's farewell, and the line every church hall has had on a wall. Note that it is a demand for decision, not encouragement.

5.h: Are you for us or for our enemies
5.t: The commander of the LORD's army answers neither. The question was the wrong one, which is worth remembering.

6.t: Seven days of marching and no fighting until the walls fall. Rahab and her family are spared, as promised.

See the note at Deuteronomy 7 for the fuller discussion. Note in this chapter that Rahab, a Canaanite, is spared because she turned to Israel's God, and she ends up in the line of Jesus. The judgement was on a people's settled rebellion rather than on ethnicity, and the door was open to anyone who turned. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

7.t: One man's theft and the defeat of the whole nation. Joshua's assumption that God had failed them is corrected sharply. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

23.t: Joshua's assessment at the end of his life, offered as the basis for the warning that follows.

3.t: The Jordan does not stop until their feet touch the water. Obedience precedes the parting.

4.t: Set up so that children would ask what they mean. Almost every memorial in the Old Testament exists to prompt a question.

8.t: Every word, to the whole assembly including women, children and foreigners. Joshua stops a military campaign to do it.

9.t: Mouldy bread and worn sandals, and the fatal line in verse 14: they did not enquire of the LORD.

10.t: A poetic citation from the Book of Jashar embedded in the narrative. How literally to read it has been argued for centuries; the text itself calls it a day like no other.

14.t: Caleb at eighty-five, asking for the hardest ground because of a promise made forty-five years earlier.

21.h: Not one of the good promises failed
21.t: The writer's summary, and the sentence the rest of the Old Testament keeps measuring Israel against.

11.t: The text presents a sweeping victory, yet Judges shows much of the land still unconquered. Scholars read the summaries here as ancient war rhetoric rather than a literal count. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

12.t: A list of defeated rulers. What was promised in Genesis 15 is recorded as fulfilled, name by name.

13.t: God tells an old Joshua that there is still land to take. The victories were real and incomplete.

15.t: The largest allotment, and the tribe of David. Verse 63: they could not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, which David would take generations later.

16.t: They did not dislodge the Canaanites in Gezer. The pattern of incomplete obedience begins to be recorded.

17.t: The tribe complains its land is too small; Joshua tells them to go and clear the hill country themselves.

18.t: Seven tribes have not taken their land. Joshua's rebuke is to people sitting on a promise.

19.t: He receives his inheritance last, after everyone else. Leadership that takes its share at the end.

20.t: Named and located, and open to the foreigner as well as the Israelite.

22.t: A near civil war over a misunderstanding, resolved because someone asked before attacking. A model for handling suspicion between brothers.

2.t: A generation arises that does not know the LORD, and the pattern begins: abandon, oppression, cry, deliverer, relapse.

6.t: Addressed as a mighty warrior while hiding in a winepress. The gap between what God calls him and what he is doing is the joke and the point.

21.h: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes
21.t: The last verse of the book, and its verdict.

4.t: A prophet leading a reluctant general, and the decisive blow struck by a woman with a tent peg. Chapter 5 sets the same events to poetry.

7.t: God reduces the army twice so Israel cannot claim the credit. The stated reason is in verse 2.

11.t: One of the darkest passages in Scripture. The text reports it without approving it, which is how Judges works throughout. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

16.t: Gifted, undisciplined and finally blind in an enemy temple. Hebrews 11 lists him by faith, which should make us careful about how we read that chapter.

19.t: The worst chapter in the Bible, and it is there to show what Israel had become. Read it with the refrain about no king in mind. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.h: They did not drive them out
1.t: A list of failures repeated seven times. The book's problems all trace back to this chapter.

3.t: A left-handed man, a concealed blade and a very physical assassination. Judges does not tidy its deliverers.

8.t: He refuses the crown with the right words and then makes a golden object that Israel prostitutes itself to. The failure comes immediately after the victory.

9.t: Gideon's son murders seventy of his brothers. Jotham's fable about the trees choosing a king is the earliest parable in Scripture.

13.t: The angel appears twice to the wife and not to Manoah, who asks how to raise the boy. It is the most carefully prepared birth in the book, and it goes wrong anyway.

17.t: A man makes an idol, ordains his own son, then hires a wandering Levite and concludes the LORD will be good to him. Religion entirely on his own terms.

5.t: One of the oldest poems in the Bible. It celebrates the tribes who came and shames those who stayed by their sheepfolds.

10.h: He could bear Israel's misery no longer
10.t: After telling them to cry to the gods they had chosen, God relents because of their suffering. Mercy that outruns justice.

12.t: Jephthah's men kill Ephraimites who cannot pronounce a word correctly. Israel is now fighting itself, and the book is sliding.

14.t: He demands a Philistine wife and it ends in a riddle, a betrayal and thirty dead men. The text says the LORD was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, which does not mean it approved of Samson. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

15.t: A thousand men killed. Then Samson, parched, cries out to God — the first time he prays in the story.

18.t: They steal Micah's idol and his priest and settle in a peaceful city by force. The priest, verse 30 reveals, was a grandson of Moses.

20.t: The tribes nearly wipe out Benjamin. The book is showing the depth of the collapse, not recommending anything in it. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: Ruth's pledge to Naomi is covenant language, spoken by a Moabite to an Israelite with nothing to offer her.

4.t: The quiet story ends by naming David. Providence has been running through it the whole time without announcing itself.

2.t: Ruth works in the field of a man who turns out to be a kinsman-redeemer. The law of gleaning in Leviticus 19 is the mechanism of the whole book.

3.t: A risky, deliberate approach. Boaz's response protects her reputation as well as her future.

3.h: Speak, for your servant is listening
3.t: The word of the LORD was rare in those days. Samuel does not recognise the voice and has to be told what to say.

8.t: God tells Samuel it is himself they are rejecting, then grants the request with a warning about what kings take. Both halves matter.

16.h: Man looks at the outward appearance
16.t: Spoken while Samuel is admiring Eliab. The LORD looks at the heart.

17.t: Read it as a story about God rather than about courage — David's speech in verses 45 to 47 makes the point explicitly.
David's speech is the interpretation of the whole story: the battle is the LORD's.

2.t: Mary's Magnificat draws on it heavily — the proud scattered, the hungry filled, the barren given children.

15.h: To obey is better than sacrifice
15.t: Samuel's verdict on Saul. The chapter is hard reading and the command in it is among the most difficult in Scripture; the verdict on partial obedience is the part that carries forward. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

24.t: He could kill him and does not, because of the anointing. Then his conscience troubles him even for cutting the robe.

1.t: Bitter in soul, praying so intensely that Eli assumes she is drunk. She gives the child back.

13.t: He does not wait the seven days. Samuel's verdict — a man after God's own heart — is about David before David appears.

18.t: He gives David his robe and his weapons, which is a prince handing over the succession. Saul's jealousy starts the same chapter.

28.t: Saul consults the dead, having earlier banned it. The chapter is strange and grim and records his final collapse.

31.t: The men of Jabesh-Gilead recover his body — the town he rescued in chapter 11. A small act of decency closing a bleak book.

4.t: Israel treats the ark as a charm to win battles, and loses both the battle and the ark. God will not be used.

5.t: The Philistine god is found face down before the ark, twice, the second time broken. The ark does its own fighting.

6.t: On a cart pulled by cows that leave their calves — something only God could explain. The men of Beth Shemesh then die for looking inside it.

7.t: Thus far the LORD has helped us. A stone set up after victory, and the root of the hymn line 'here I raise my Ebenezer'.

9.t: Saul goes out to find lost animals and comes back anointed king. God's providence works through an errand.

10.t: Chosen by lot and nowhere to be found. Saul's reluctance looks like humility and turns out to be something else.

11.t: He rescues Jabesh-Gilead and refuses to execute those who opposed him. It is the man he could have remained.

12.h: Far be it from me to sin by failing to pray
12.t: Samuel's farewell. He counts it a sin not to pray for the people who rejected his leadership.

14.t: Jonathan's faith against a garrison, and Saul's foolish vow that nearly gets his own son killed.

19.t: Michal and Jonathan both protect David against their own father.

20.t: Jonathan's covenant with David, at the cost of his own succession. One of the great friendships of Scripture.

21.t: David eats it at Nob. Jesus cites this in defending his disciples on the Sabbath.

22.t: Saul massacres them. David takes responsibility for having caused it — an unusual admission.

23.h: Jonathan helped him find strength in God
23.t: He went to David in the wilderness to encourage him. One sentence describing what a friend is for.

25.t: A woman whose quick wisdom stops David from shedding blood in anger. He thanks God for her, and for being stopped.

26.h: The spear and the water jug
26.t: A second chance to kill Saul, and a second refusal. David will not take by force what God has promised.

27.t: He despairs and flees to the enemy, lying to their king. His years in the wilderness were not all faith.

29.t: The Philistine commanders refuse to let David fight Israel. A providential rejection saves him from an impossible position.

30.h: David strengthened himself in the LORD
30.t: His men are talking of stoning him. What he does first is turn to God.

7.t: A house for God becomes a house from God: a throne established forever. Every messianic expectation in the Old Testament runs through this chapter.

11.h: The year kings go to war
11.t: David stays home. Adultery, then a cover-up, then murder. The chapter ends noting that what he had done displeased the LORD.

11.h: At the time when kings go off to war
11.t: David stayed in Jerusalem. The chapter's first sentence contains its cause.

12.t: Nathan traps him with a story. The consequences are not removed by the forgiveness, and the rest of the book is them.
David gets up, washes and eats. His explanation — I will go to him, he will not return to me — is one of the earliest hints of hope beyond death.

9.t: David seeks out Jonathan's crippled son to show kindness for the sake of a covenant with a dead man. A picture of grace that the rest of the book badly needs.

23.t: The oracle of the man raised on high. He describes a ruler who governs in the fear of God, which he had mostly failed to be.

1.t: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. He mourns the man who hunted him.

6.t: Uzzah's death and David's undignified joy. Michal despises him and the narrator records his answer. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

18.t: David's grief for the son who tried to kill him. Joab's rebuke afterwards is brutal and not entirely wrong.

2.t: Shall I go up? He enquires of the LORD before moving, which Saul repeatedly did not.

3.t: The house of David grew stronger and the house of Saul weaker. The transition took years, not a moment.

5.t: At thirty, after years of waiting. Verse 12 notes he knew the LORD had established him for the sake of the people.

15.t: He stole the hearts of Israel by standing at the gate. David leaves the city barefoot and weeping.

16.t: David refuses to let him be killed: perhaps the LORD will look on my misery. Remarkable restraint from a king in flight.

22.t: Nearly identical to Psalm 18. Two copies preserved, one in the history and one in the hymnbook.

24.h: I will not offer what costs me nothing
24.t: David's refusal of a free threshing floor, on the site where the temple would stand.

4.t: David executes the killers who expected a reward. He will not accept a throne won by treachery.

8.t: David's reign at its height, summarised in the two words the prophets will keep using.

10.t: A diplomatic insult escalates into war. The chapter sets the scene for David's failure in chapter 11.

13.t: A terrible chapter of rape and revenge within David's own family, and David's failure to act. Nathan's word in chapter 12 is being fulfilled. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

14.t: So that a banished person does not remain banished. The wise woman of Tekoa speaks better than she knows about God's grace.

17.t: Hushai's counsel prevails over Ahithophel's, and the writer says why. Providence working through advice given in a council.

19.t: David grieves Absalom so publicly that his loyal soldiers feel ashamed of winning. Joab is blunt and right.

20.t: The kingdom nearly splits again. A wise woman in a besieged town saves it by negotiation.

21.t: A hard chapter involving the execution of Saul's descendants. Rizpah's vigil over the bodies is what moves David to act with decency. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

3.h: Ask what I shall give you
3.t: Solomon asks for a discerning heart. The book will show how little that protected him.
The famous judgement. Solomon's wisdom is demonstrated rather than described.

8.t: At the temple's dedication he asks the honest question — will God really dwell on earth? — and anticipates exile.

8.h: Will God really dwell on earth
8.t: Solomon asks the honest question at the dedication of the building he has just spent seven years on.

18.t: Elijah against the prophets of Baal. The mockery in verse 27 is savage and is in the text.

18.h: A cloud the size of a man's hand
18.t: Elijah prays seven times and sends the servant back each time. Persistence after the public victory.

19.t: Straight after the triumph, Elijah wants to die. God's response is sleep, food, and then a quiet voice rather than a rebuke.
He burns his ploughing equipment to cook the oxen. Leaving the old work is made literally irreversible.

11.t: Seven hundred wives, and his heart turned. The wisest man in the world fails exactly where Deuteronomy 17 warned kings would.

12.t: Rehoboam takes the young men's advice over the elders'. One bad decision, and a division that never heals.

17.t: Fed by ravens, then by a woman with nothing. Jesus cites this episode at Nazareth.

21.t: Judicial murder for a plot of land. Elijah confronts Ahab, and Ahab's partial repentance delays the judgement — which is worth noticing.

1.t: David is old and a son crowns himself. Nathan and Bathsheba act quickly, and Solomon is anointed instead.

6.t: Seven years, and the chronology in verse 1 anchors Israel's history to the exodus.

10.t: She comes to test him and leaves overwhelmed. Jesus cites her against his own generation.

13.h: The man of God from Judah
13.t: He obeys, is deceived by an older prophet, disobeys, and dies. An uncomfortable chapter about taking instructions from the wrong source.

2.t: Walk in God's ways — and then settle these old scores. The mixture is recorded honestly.

4.t: Three thousand proverbs and a thousand songs, and knowledge of plants and animals. Wisdom is presented as broad, not merely religious.

5.t: The temple built with Gentile timber and skill.

7.t: Thirteen years for his palace against seven for the temple. The writer notes it without comment.

9.t: God's warning: if you turn away, this house will become a heap of rubble. Blessing and threat in the same speech.

14.t: She visits a blind prophet who knows who she is before she speaks.

15.t: He removes his own grandmother from her position for making an idol. Reform that reaches into his own family.

16.t: He did more evil than all before him, marrying Jezebel and serving Baal. The stage is set for Elijah.

20.t: The Syrians decide Israel's God only rules the mountains. God defeats them in the plain to prove otherwise.

22.t: Four hundred prophets say what the king wants; one tells the truth and is imprisoned. The vision of the lying spirit is among the strangest in Scripture. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

5.t: A Syrian general healed after being insulted by the simplicity of the instruction. Jesus cites this at Nazareth.

17.t: The writer stops the narrative to explain the theology of the exile in one long paragraph.

25.t: The temple burned, the walls broken, the people taken. The book ends with a released king eating at a foreign table — a very small door left open.

2.t: Elisha asks for a double portion, the inheritance of a firstborn son rather than twice the power.

6.t: The servant sees only the army. Elisha prays and he sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Then the captured raiders are fed and sent home.

18.t: He removed the high places and broke up the bronze serpent, which the people had been burning incense to. Even a genuine relic can become an idol.

19.h: Spreading the letter before the LORD
19.t: Hezekiah takes the threat into the temple and lays it out. A model of what to do with a letter you cannot answer.

22.h: The book found in the temple
22.t: Josiah tears his clothes when it is read, because nobody had known what it said. Reform follows from rediscovery.

4.t: It keeps flowing while there are jars to fill. The limit is set by what she gathered.
She builds a room for the prophet and later loses the son she was given. Her refusal to be comforted takes her straight to Elisha.

7.t: They find the enemy camp abandoned and say to each other: this is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves.

13.t: The king strikes three times and Elisha is angry that he stopped. A strange episode about half-hearted obedience.

20.t: Hezekiah is told to put his house in order, weeps, and is given an extension. Read chapter 20 to the end before deciding it was a blessing.

23.t: The most thorough reform in Israel's history, and the writer still says God's anger was not turned away. Reform from the top does not change hearts.

24.t: The first deportations, including the young men Daniel is among.

1.h: Is there no God in Israel
1.t: Ahaziah sends to consult Baal-Zebub. Elijah's question exposes it.

3.t: Water comes without wind or rain. The preparation is commanded before the provision appears.

8.t: She arrives at the exact moment the king is hearing her story. Providence in timing.

9.t: Her death fulfils Elijah's word precisely.

10.t: He destroys Baal worship but keeps the golden calves. Zeal that stops exactly where it would cost him.

11.t: A queen kills the royal family, and one baby is hidden in the temple for six years. The line of David survives by a single child.

12.t: A chest with a hole in the lid, and workers so honest no accounts were needed.

14.t: He spares the sons of his father's assassins, obeying the law of Moses. Then pride leads him into an unnecessary war.

15.t: Several reigns in a few verses, with assassinations and short tenures. Israel's end is coming fast.

16.t: He copies a pagan altar from Damascus and installs it in the temple.

21.t: The worst king in Judah's history, fifty-five years long. Chronicles records his repentance; Kings records the damage. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

17.t: Chronicles retells 2 Samuel 7 for the returned exiles, for whom the promise to David was the reason to hope at all.
David's response to the covenant is to sit down and ask why. Neither triumph nor false modesty.

29.t: Everything comes from your hand, and of your own we have given you. The theology of giving in two sentences.

29.h: Who am I, and who are my people
29.t: Everything comes from your hand and we have given you only what comes from your hand. Said while giving on an enormous scale.

21.t: David counts his fighting men and is judged for it. He refuses to offer a sacrifice that costs him nothing.

28.h: Know the God of your father
28.t: And serve him with wholehearted devotion, for the LORD searches every heart. David's charge to Solomon.

1.t: Chronicles opens with genealogies from Adam onward, written for returned exiles who needed to know they were still the same people.

10.t: Chronicles gives the theological summary Samuel leaves implicit: he was unfaithful and did not enquire of the LORD.

11.t: Three men break through enemy lines for a drink and David pours it out rather than drink it. Loyalty honoured by refusing to consume it.

16.t: A psalm assembled from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106, sung when the ark came to Jerusalem.

22.t: David is told he will not build the temple. He spends the rest of his life collecting materials for the son who will.

4.t: Two verses inside nine chapters of names. It became a bestseller in 2000; in context it is one man among hundreds.

13.t: The ark moved on a new cart rather than carried by Levites, as chapter 15 later acknowledges.

15.t: David says no one but the Levites may carry the ark, because we did not enquire how to do it in the prescribed way.

23.t: Detailed rotas for worship. Chronicles cares about this because its readers were rebuilding exactly this.

2.t: The genealogy slows down as it reaches David. The writer is heading for the king.

3.t: Traced past the exile. The line survived.

5.t: A tribal war won because they trusted him, noted in the middle of a genealogy.

6.t: Heman, Asaph and Ethan, whose names head many psalms.

7.t: Recorded even though the north had been destroyed. The writer insists all twelve belong.

8.t: The genealogy of the first king, preserved alongside David's.

9.t: The first to return are listed. The genealogies were written for exactly these people.

12.t: The men of Issachar knew what Israel should do. A phrase often borrowed, and rightly.

14.t: Twice, and receives different instructions each time. Past guidance does not replace present asking.

18.t: David's reign summarised, as in 2 Samuel 8.

19.t: Retold without the Bathsheba episode, which Chronicles omits. The Chronicler is writing to encourage, not to record everything.

20.t: The Chronicler skips straight from the siege to its end.

24.t: Twenty-four courses. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, served in the course of Abijah.

25.t: Music in worship is described as a form of prophecy. Worship leaders were appointed by lot, young and old alike.

26.t: Even the doorkeepers are named. Chronicles honours ordinary service.

27.t: Twelve units, each serving one month. Administration recorded as part of faithful kingship.

7.t: The people fall face down on the pavement. Chronicles adds this detail that Kings does not have.

Written to Israel under a specific covenant, and frequently applied to modern nations in ways the text does not support. The principle of humility and repentance stands; the national promise was theirs. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

36.h: He sent word again and again
36.t: Because he had pity on his people — until there was no remedy. The verdict on the whole history.
The Hebrew Bible ends here, with permission to go home. That is a deliberate place to stop.

16.h: The eyes of the LORD range
16.t: Looking for those whose hearts are fully committed. Said as a rebuke to a king who trusted an alliance instead.

20.h: We do not know what to do
20.t: Jehoshaphat's prayer facing invasion, ending with that admission and with eyes on God. The battle is won by singers going out in front.

34.t: He began seeking God at sixteen and purging idolatry at twenty. Chronicles gives his age deliberately.

1.t: Solomon asks for wisdom to govern, and is given wealth as well. Chronicles frames it as a test he passed.

5.t: The priests could not perform their service. The singers were in unison praising God when it happened.

6.t: Longer here than in Kings, and it anticipates exile and asks that prayers turned toward this place be heard.

14.t: Asa's prayer before battle: it is nothing for you to help the powerless against the mighty.

15.h: Be strong and do not give up
15.t: Azariah's word to Asa. The reform that follows is genuine and, as chapter 16 shows, not permanent.

17.t: Jehoshaphat sends officials and Levites out with the Book of the Law. A deliberate programme of teaching rather than a one-off reform.

26.t: Uzziah's pride led to his downfall. He burns incense in the temple and is struck with leprosy. Chronicles is repeatedly interested in what success does to kings.

30.t: Held late and by people who were not properly purified. Hezekiah prays that God would pardon everyone who sets their heart on seeking him, and God heard.

33.t: The worst king in Judah's history, taken to Babylon with a hook in his nose, humbles himself and is restored. Chronicles alone records it.

2.h: Who can build a house for him
2.t: Solomon asks it before he starts building. Humility at the beginning of the project.

3.t: Where Abraham offered Isaac, and where David saw the angel. Chronicles connects them deliberately.

4.t: Bronze sea and lampstands. Everything costly, all of it eventually carried to Babylon.

8.t: Building, trade and administration at the height of the kingdom.

9.t: Chronicles keeps the visit and omits Solomon's decline entirely.

10.t: Rehoboam's harshness divides the kingdom. The writer says the turn of events was from God.

11.t: Faithful Levites leave their land in the north to worship in Jerusalem. Faith costing property.

12.t: When Rehoboam abandons God, Egypt invades; when he humbles himself, destruction is withheld.

13.t: A king arguing theology to an enemy army before battle.

18.t: Told as in Kings, with Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab condemned in chapter 19.

19.t: Consider carefully what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD. Justice treated as an act of worship.

21.t: He murders his brothers and dies to no one's regret. Chronicles records it bluntly.

22.t: The same crisis as 2 Kings 11 — the line of David down to one hidden child.

23.t: Jehoiada the priest restores the rightful king.

24.t: Joash kills the son of the priest who saved him. Jesus refers to this murder in Matthew 23.

25.t: He does right, but not wholeheartedly. Chronicles' verdict on a divided heart.

27.t: Because he walked steadfastly before the LORD.

28.t: He shuts the temple doors. Israel's northern soldiers return captives from Judah after a prophet rebukes them — mercy from an unexpected side.

29.t: In the first month of his first year. Reform was his first act, not an afterthought.

31.t: And he prospered. Chronicles' summary of a faithful king.

32.t: After his healing, his heart was proud. Even the best kings failed afterwards.

35.t: None like it since Samuel. And then, in chapter 35:20–27, he dies in a battle he was warned not to fight.

3.t: The older men who had seen the first temple wept at the foundation of the second. Both sounds were heard together and could not be distinguished.

7.t: To study, to do, and to teach — in that order. The best one-verse description of a teacher in Scripture.

9.t: He tears his clothes and prays in the first person plural about sins he did not commit. Intercession of a kind that is rarely modelled now.

1.h: The LORD moved the heart of Cyrus
1.t: A pagan emperor's decree described as God's doing. Isaiah had named him long before.

4.t: First an offer to help, then discouragement, then a letter to the king. The work stops for years.

5.t: Haggai and Zechariah get the building restarted. Preaching with a practical result.

6.t: Dedicated with joy, and the Passover kept. Note verse 22: God changed the attitude of the king of Assyria.

8.t: Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him, so he fasts instead of requesting an escort. Integrity with a cost attached.

10.t: The dissolving of intermarriages. A hard chapter, and the text records the weeping rather than presenting it as simple.

2.t: Nearly fifty thousand names and numbers. Each family who came back is recorded, as if each one mattered.

1.t: He hears the news and sits down and weeps for days before doing anything. Then he plans.

2.t: He prays to God and then speaks to the king in the same breath. Faith and nerve are not alternatives here.

4.h: We prayed and posted a guard
4.t: The whole book's method in one verse. Nehemiah never treats prayer and practical action as alternatives; faced with a real threat to the builders, he does both at once, and the work goes on.

8.t: Ezra reads, the Levites explain, and the people weep and are told not to. The joy of the LORD is your strength arrives as a correction.

5.h: Charging interest to your own people
5.t: Nehemiah is angry, calls an assembly, and makes the nobles return what they have taken. Reform of a community's economics, not only its walls.

6.h: I am doing a great work
6.t: Four invitations to come down to the plain, each refused with the same sentence. Distraction dressed as reasonableness.

13.t: Nehemiah returns to find the reforms undone. The book ends with the work incomplete, which is honest.

3.t: Named families, each building near their own house. The nobles of Tekoa would not put their shoulders to the work, and that is recorded too.

7.t: The list from Ezra 2 repeated. Nehemiah populates the city only after he knows who belongs.

9.t: Israel's history retold as a prayer, from Abraham to the present, acknowledging God just in everything that happened.

10.t: Specific commitments: marriage, Sabbath, tithes, the temple. They put it in writing.

11.t: The people blessed those who volunteered to live in the city. Staying was a sacrifice.

12.t: Two choirs on the walls, and the rejoicing heard far away.

4.h: For such a time as this
4.t: Mordecai's argument has two halves: deliverance will come from somewhere, and you may have been placed here for this. Providence and responsibility together.

6.t: The king cannot sleep, has the records read, and the whole plot turns. God is never named and is not hard to find.

1.t: A queen deposed for disobeying a drunk king, and an empire-wide decree about wives. The book's comedy is very dark.

2.t: The text does not present this as a romance. She is conscripted into a harem and conceals her identity on Mordecai's instruction.

3.t: Genocide authorised over one man's refusal to bow, and the chapter ends with the king and Haman sitting down to drink while the city is bewildered.

5.t: She approaches uninvited, which carried a death penalty, and then invites him to dinner rather than making her request.

7.t: The reversal the whole book has been building. Haman dies on the structure he built for Mordecai.

8.t: The first cannot be revoked, so a second is issued. Many peoples became Jews because fear had seized them.

9.t: The festival established to remember it, still kept. A book with no mention of God produces a permanent act of thanksgiving.

10.t: He seeks the good of his people and speaks for their welfare. The book ends with a Jew second to the king, as Genesis ended with Joseph.

1.t: The reader is shown the heavenly scene; Job never is. That asymmetry is the key to the book.
After losing everything, in the same breath as tearing his robe. The narrator adds that in all this Job did not sin.

2.h: Shall we accept good and not trouble
2.t: Job's answer to his wife. The narrator again notes he did not sin in what he said.
Job's friends do their best work before they open their mouths.

38.t: Four chapters of questions about creation, and no explanation of the suffering. What Job receives is not information but God.
When I laid the earth's foundation. God answers a question about suffering with a question about creation.

42.h: I had heard, now I see
42.t: Job repents of what he said, not of what he was accused of. The friends are told they have not spoken rightly, and Job prays for them.
God says they have not spoken rightly, and Job must pray for them. Restoration comes after intercession for the people who wounded him.

3.t: Not God, but the day he was born. The book allows the full weight of that without correcting him.

19.h: I know that my Redeemer lives
19.t: Spoken at the lowest point of the book, not at the resolution. Handel set it; Job had no evidence for it.

23.t: Forward, backward, left, right — and then: but he knows the way that I take. Faith without felt presence.

4.t: Kindly at first, and built on a vision he had at night. His logic — the innocent do not perish — is the assumption the book exists to demolish.

9.h: If only there were a mediator
9.t: Job wishes for someone to lay a hand on them both. The New Testament answers a question Job could only ask.

14.h: If a man dies, will he live again
14.t: Asked, not answered. Job's honesty is what makes the book usable to people in the middle of grief.

28.t: A poem on the inaccessibility of wisdom, ending with the only answer available: the fear of the Lord.

31.t: A remarkable ethical self-examination, including a covenant with his eyes and his treatment of servants and the poor.

40.t: God's second speech asks whether Job would condemn him in order to justify himself. That is the actual charge.

5.h: He wounds but he binds up
5.t: Eliphaz saying something true inside an argument that is wrong. Not every sentence from a bad counsellor is false.

6.h: A despairing man should have the devotion of his friends
6.t: Job's complaint about how he is being treated.

7.t: I will speak out in the anguish of my spirit. Job claims the right to complain.

8.t: Blunter than Eliphaz: your children sinned and God gave them over. Said to a man whose ten children have just died.

10.t: Job argues from being made by God to being owed an explanation by him.

11.h: Can you fathom the mysteries of God
11.t: Zophar asks a good question for the wrong reason, and God asks it again at the end for the right one.

12.h: To God belong wisdom and power
12.t: Job knows the orthodox answers as well as his friends do, and says so.

13.h: Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him
13.t: The Hebrew is difficult and can also read 'I have no hope'. Both renderings are defensible and translations differ. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

16.t: One who pleads for me as a man pleads for his friend. Job keeps reaching for a mediator.

17.t: Short, flat, and without any attempt to soften it.

21.h: Why do the wicked live on
21.t: Job's counter-evidence against his friends' whole system.

27.h: I will not deny my integrity
27.t: Job refuses to confess sins he has not committed in order to fit their theory.

29.h: How I long for the months gone by
29.t: Job remembers respect, usefulness and family. Grief includes the loss of who you were.

30.h: I cry out to you but you do not answer
30.t: The contrast with chapter 29 is the whole point.

32.t: A younger man who waited and then speaks for six chapters. Interpreters divide on whether he is right; notably God neither rebukes nor commends him.

39.t: Mountain goats, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the warhorse, the hawk. Creatures useless to humans, delighted in by God.

41.t: A whole chapter on a creature nobody can control. The argument is cumulative: you cannot manage this, and I made it.

15.t: Sharper this time: Job's own words condemn him. The friends are escalating because Job will not accept their explanation.

18.h: Bildad on the fate of the wicked
18.t: A catalogue of disasters that fall on the ungodly — delivered to a man suffering exactly those disasters.

20.t: The wicked's prosperity is brief. True as a general observation and cruel as an accusation.

22.t: Having no evidence, he supplies it: you must have stripped the naked and refused water to the weary. Theory driving the facts.

24.h: Why does the Almighty not set times
24.t: Job describes the poor exploited while God appears to do nothing. The question is left standing.

25.t: Six verses, and the friends' arguments run out. How can a man be righteous before God? A good question, badly used.

26.t: Job says all creation is only the edge of God's ways, a whisper. He knows God's greatness as well as his friends do.

33.t: Elihu suggests suffering may be God's instruction rather than punishment. Interpreters are divided on whether he advances the argument. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

34.h: Far be it from God to do evil
34.t: Elihu defends God's justice. His conclusion is orthodox; his treatment of Job is harsh.

35.t: People cry out under oppression but do not ask where God is. Elihu names a real failure in how people suffer.

36.h: He delivers the afflicted by their affliction
36.t: A compact statement of how suffering can be used, set in the build-up to God's own speech.

37.t: Elihu ends with the storm — the very storm from which God is about to speak.

1.t: The fear of the LORD is the starting point rather than the conclusion — everything in the book assumes it.
Personified as a woman shouting in public. The rebuke is that people ignore what is freely available.

3.h: Lean not on your own understanding
3.t: Trust with the whole heart, acknowledge him, and he makes the paths straight. Frequently quoted as a promise about outcomes; it is about direction.

3.h: Honour the LORD with your wealth
3.t: Firstfruits rather than leftovers. The proverb assumes giving comes off the top.

3.h: Do not despise the LORD's discipline
3.t: Quoted in Hebrews 12. He disciplines those he loves, as a father the son he delights in.

8.t: A poetic figure, presented as a woman, who was beside God at creation. Reading her as a created being who made the world is a great deal of weight for a figure of speech to carry. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

31.t: An acrostic poem. She trades, buys land, plants a vineyard and speaks with wisdom. Not a checklist so much as a portrait of strength.

4.t: Above all else, because everything you do flows from it. The chapter is a father's instruction to a son.

6.t: Practical wisdom about work, followed by the sluggard's slow slide into poverty.
A list God hates, and six of the seven concern how people treat one another with words.

10.t: From here the book is mostly two-line sayings setting the wise against the foolish. Read a few at a time rather than in bulk.

13.t: The companion of fools suffers harm. As blunt a statement about friendship as Scripture gives.

15.t: Turns away wrath. The chapter has a dozen sayings about speech and most of them are about restraint.

16.t: But the LORD establishes his steps. Verse 18 — pride before destruction — is from the same chapter.

18.t: Is folly and shame. Verse 17 makes the same point: the first to present his case seems right until another comes and questions him.

22.t: A proverb rather than a guarantee, which matters enormously to parents whose children have walked away.

27.t: Are faithful; an enemy's kisses are profuse. Verse 17 — iron sharpens iron — is the group's reason for asking each other hard questions.

11.t: Where there is no guidance a people falls. Repeated at 15:22 and 24:6 — Proverbs rarely says anything three times by accident.

12.h: A fool is right in his own eyes
12.t: But the wise listen to advice. Probably the single most repeated idea in the book.

14.t: There is a way that appears right to a man, and its end is death. Stated twice, here and at 16:25.

17.h: A friend loves at all times
17.t: And a brother is born for a time of adversity. The verse this group could put on the wall.

19.t: But the LORD's purpose prevails. Sovereignty stated in one line of Hebrew poetry.

20.t: Proverbs is repeatedly blunt about drink, without being prohibitionist.
The purposes of a man's heart are deep waters, but one who has insight draws them out. A description of what good listening does.

24.h: Though the righteous fall seven times
24.t: They rise again. Failure is assumed rather than excluded.

28.t: Does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy. The Proverbs version of 1 John 1:9.

29.h: Fear of man is a snare
29.t: But whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe. A verse about the actual reason most men stay quiet.

2.h: If you search for it as for silver
2.t: Wisdom requires effort and seeking — and then verse 6 says the LORD gives it. Both are true.

5.h: Drink water from your own cistern
5.t: A frank warning against adultery and a celebration of faithfulness within marriage.

7.t: A story told from a window: a youth walking toward a house he should avoid, at dusk. The warning is about drifting, not deciding.

9.t: Wisdom and Folly both set a table and call out to the passers-by. The reader has to choose which house to enter.

21.t: Is a stream of water in the LORD's hand. Even rulers are within his direction.

23.t: The clearest description of drunkenness in Scripture, ending with the drunk man wanting another drink.

25.t: Give him food. Paul quotes this in Romans 12 as the way to overcome evil with good.

26.h: Answer a fool — and do not
26.t: Two contradictory proverbs placed side by side on purpose. Wisdom knows which situation calls for which.

30.t: Agur's prayer: give me only my daily bread, lest I become proud or desperate.

1.t: The word usually translated 'meaningless' means breath or mist — fleeting and hard to grasp rather than pointless. That distinction changes the whole book.

3.t: Often read at funerals as comfort; in context it is about the limits of human control. Verse 11 — he has set eternity in the human heart — is the ache the book is describing.

12.t: Fear God and keep his commandments. After eleven chapters of dismantling every alternative, the ending is deliberately plain.

5.t: Let your words be few. Advice about worship from the most sceptical book in the Bible, and better for it.

9.t: Eat your bread with joy. The Preacher's conclusion is not despair but the ordinary goodness of a day well used.

2.t: Pleasure, building, wealth, wisdom. The Preacher concludes that he hated life, and then that eating and drinking and finding satisfaction in work is from God's hand. Both sentences are in the same chapter.

4.t: If either falls, one can help the other up. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken. Usually read at weddings; written about ordinary companionship.

7.h: Better to go to a house of mourning
7.t: Because death is the destiny of everyone, and the living should take it to heart. Bracing rather than morbid.

11.h: Cast your bread upon the waters
11.t: Sow in the morning and do not be idle in the evening, because you do not know which will succeed. An argument for acting under uncertainty.

6.t: A man given everything but not the ability to enjoy it. The Preacher calls it a grievous evil.

8.h: Though a sinner does evil a hundred times
8.t: I know it will go well for those who fear God. The Preacher holds his observations and his faith together.

10.t: More strength is needed, but wisdom brings success. Practical sense about sharpening your tools.

2.t: Read allegorically for most of church history and plainly for the last two centuries. The plain sense should not be explained away: desire within marriage is treated as good.

8.t: Love as a seal, jealousy fierce as the grave, and many waters unable to quench it. The high point of the book.

1.t: The Hebrew superlative — the best of all songs. It opens in the woman's voice, and she speaks more than he does throughout.

3.t: A dream sequence. The refrain about not awakening love before it pleases appears three times in the book.

4.t: Imagery from flocks, towers and gardens. It reads strangely now and would have read as high compliment then.

5.t: She hesitates and misses him, then searches and is beaten by the watchmen. The book does not present desire as simple.

6.h: I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine
6.t: The book's central claim, stated three times in slightly different forms.

7.t: The same Hebrew word used in Genesis 3:16 and 4:7, here turned to something good.

1.t: An ox knows its owner; Israel does not know. Isaiah opens by calling heaven and earth as witnesses.

1.h: I have had enough of burnt offerings
1.t: God rejects worship offered by people who ignore the orphan and the widow. Then: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.

6.t: Isaiah sees the LORD on a throne and is undone. John says Isaiah saw Christ's glory and spoke of him.
His first reaction to seeing God is not comfort but ruin, and specifically about his lips — the tool of his trade.
A message that will harden rather than convert. Quoted by Jesus, Paul and John.

7.t: The sign given to Ahaz. Matthew reads it as fulfilled in the virgin birth; the Hebrew word can mean young woman, and the Greek translators used the word for virgin two centuries before Christ.

9.t: Galilee of the nations named centuries before Jesus' ministry there. Matthew quotes it.

9.h: Unto us a child is born
9.t: Four titles, one of which is Mighty God — a phrase used again two chapters later, at 10:21, of the LORD himself.

40.t: The turn of the book. The voice in the wilderness is applied to John the Baptist by all four Gospels.
A sustained argument for God's incomparability, ending with the stars called out by name. It is the ground for the promise in verse 31.

40.h: They will run and not grow weary
40.t: The chapter that begins with comfort ends with strength, and the argument between them is about who God is.

42.t: The Servant will not break a bruised reed. The Father's words at Jesus' baptism draw on verse 1.

42.h: A bruised reed he will not break
42.t: The Servant's gentleness stated before his power. Matthew applies it to Jesus' habit of avoiding confrontation.

45.h: I am the LORD, and there is no other
45.t: Including the difficult line about creating light and darkness, prosperity and disaster. Isaiah refuses a tidy dualism.
God swears by himself that to him every knee will bow. Paul applies these words to Jesus in Philippians 2 and to God in Romans 14.

53.t: Pierced for our transgressions, the punishment that brought us peace, the LORD laying on him the iniquity of us all. The clearest Old Testament statement of substitution, and the passage the Ethiopian was reading in Acts 8.
Each of us turned to our own way, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all. Substitution stated in a single verse.
The hardest line in the chapter, and the one that makes the cross purposeful rather than tragic. He will see his offspring and be satisfied.

55.t: Buy without money. Grace stated seven centuries before the cross.
And the word that goes out and does not return empty. The passage is about God's purposes outrunning our understanding of them.

61.h: The year of the Lord's favour
61.t: The passage Jesus read at Nazareth, stopping mid-sentence before the day of vengeance.

11.t: The line of David cut down to a stump, and a shoot coming from it. The Spirit rests on him, and the peace described reaches the whole creation.

25.t: A banquet for all peoples, the shroud over the nations removed, and every tear wiped away. Revelation 21 quotes it.

30.t: In repentance and rest is your salvation — and then the honest note: but you would have none of it.

35.t: A highway called the Way of Holiness. Jesus alludes to verses 5 and 6 when John's disciples ask if he is the one.

43.h: I have called you by name
43.t: Passing through waters and fire. The promise is presence, not exemption.
You are my witnesses, so that you may know and believe that I am he. John puts the same phrase on Jesus' lips in chapter 13.

49.t: The Servant's task is too small if it is only to restore Israel. Paul and Barnabas quote it in Acts 13.
Can a mother forget her child? Even she may — I will not.

58.t: Not bowed heads but loosing chains, sharing bread, housing the homeless. One of the sharpest passages in the prophets on worship divorced from justice.

64.t: All our righteous acts. The verse is often quoted about sin; it is actually about our best efforts.

66.h: This is the one I esteem
66.t: Humble and contrite in spirit, and trembling at my word. The book ends where it began, with what God actually looks for.

14.t: Addressed to the king of Babylon, and read by many since as also describing the fall of Satan. The primary reference in the text is the king.

26.t: You will keep in perfect peace the one whose mind is steadfast. The Hebrew literally doubles the word for peace.

41.h: Do not fear, for I am with you
41.t: I will strengthen you, help you, uphold you with my righteous right hand. Three verbs, all in the first person.

44.h: The man who makes an idol
44.t: He burns half the log to cook his dinner and worships the other half. The mockery is deliberate and devastating.
God says he stretched out the heavens by himself and spread out the earth alone, and then asks who was with him. The question is rhetorical and it excludes help.

48.t: I have refined you, though not as silver. Testing described as purposeful rather than punitive.

52.t: Of those who bring good news. Paul quotes it in Romans 10 as the basis of preaching.
Chapter 53 actually starts here, with the Servant raised and lifted up — the same words used of the LORD in chapter 6.

57.t: Who lives with the contrite and lowly in spirit. Both halves of the sentence matter.

59.t: The arm of the LORD is not short; sin has separated. The diagnosis before the remedy.

65.h: New heavens and a new earth
65.t: Isaiah's vision that Revelation 21 draws on directly.

2.t: All nations stream to God's mountain and learn war no more. The same vision appears in Micah 4.

3.t: God takes away every support of the city. Verse 12: youths oppress my people, women rule over them — a picture of collapse, not a rule about leadership.

4.t: A canopy of glory over Zion, like the cloud in the wilderness. Restoration after cleansing.

5.t: God planted it carefully and it produced wild grapes. He looked for justice and saw bloodshed — a pun in the Hebrew.

8.h: Do not fear what they fear
8.t: Peter quotes this in his first letter. The LORD is the one to regard as holy.

10.h: Assyria, the rod of my anger
10.t: God uses Assyria, and then judges it for its pride. He uses nations without approving them.

12.h: In that day you will say
12.t: A short hymn of praise closing the first section. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.

13.t: The first oracle against the nations. Babylon here is both a real empire and a symbol, as in Revelation.

15.h: My heart cries out for Moab
15.t: The prophet grieves over the enemy he pronounces judgement on.

16.t: In the middle of an oracle against Moab, a promise of a just king from David's line.

17.h: You have forgotten God your Saviour
17.t: Damascus and Israel judged together for forgetting the Rock.

18.t: Even distant Cush will bring tribute to Zion. The nations are drawn in.

19.t: An astonishing promise: Egypt and Assyria worshipping alongside Israel, all three blessed. Old Testament universalism of the most striking kind.

20.t: Isaiah walks naked as a sign against trusting Egypt. The prophets performed what they preached.

21.t: Morning is coming, and also the night. An enigmatic oracle often read devotionally.

22.t: For tomorrow we die. Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 15 as the logic of a life without resurrection.

23.t: The great trading city brought low. Revelation 18's lament over Babylon draws on this chapter.

24.t: The 'Isaiah apocalypse' begins: judgement on a global scale, with God reigning on Mount Zion at the end.

27.t: The sea monster slain by God's sword. Ancient imagery of chaos used to describe God's final victory over evil.

28.t: A precious cornerstone in Zion; whoever trusts will not be dismayed. Quoted by Paul and Peter of Christ.

29.h: Their hearts are far from me
29.t: Jesus quotes it against the Pharisees in Mark 7.

31.h: Woe to those who go down to Egypt
31.t: Trusting horses and chariots rather than the Holy One of Israel.

32.h: A king will reign in righteousness
32.t: Each man like a shelter from the wind. The noble man makes noble plans.

33.h: The LORD is our judge, lawgiver, king
33.t: Three functions of government united in God.

34.t: A dark oracle using the imagery of total devastation. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

36.t: Assyria's envoy mocks trust in God in the hearing of the people on the wall. Nearly identical to 2 Kings 18.

37.t: He spreads the letter before the LORD. The answer comes through Isaiah, and 185,000 Assyrians die in the night.

38.t: Written after his recovery. For it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness.

39.t: Hezekiah displays his wealth to Babylonian envoys. Isaiah predicts Babylon will carry it all away.

46.t: The idols of Babylon are loaded onto animals; God carries his people from birth to old age.

47.t: The proud city sits in the dust. Its boast — I am, and there is none besides me — is God's own title.

50.t: He gives his back to those who strike him and his cheeks to those who pull out his beard. The Gospels' passion accounts echo it.

51.t: Consider Abraham, who was one when I called him. God's past faithfulness as the ground of present hope.

54.t: Paul quotes it in Galatians 4. My unfailing love for you will not be shaken, though the mountains depart.

56.t: Those excluded under the old law are welcomed with a name better than sons and daughters. The eunuch of Acts 8 was reading nearby.

60.t: The nations come to your light. Revelation 21 draws on the whole chapter for the new Jerusalem.

62.t: No longer called Deserted, but My Delight Is in Her. God rejoicing over his people as a bridegroom over his bride.

63.t: The warrior treading the winepress alone. Revelation 19 uses the image of the returning Christ.

1.t: Jeremiah objects that he is too young. He will be right about almost everything and heeded about nothing.
An almond branch and a boiling pot. God promises to make him a fortified city, which implies what is coming.

17.h: Like a tree planted by water
17.t: The same image as Psalm 1, and it does not promise the absence of heat but the absence of anxiety in it.
A diagnosis, not a slogan. It explains why the covenant of chapter 31 has to be internal.

29.h: Seek the peace of the city
29.t: Build houses, plant gardens, and pray for Babylon's welfare. Instructions for living faithfully in a place you did not choose.
Spoken to exiles who have just been told to settle down and build houses because they will be there seventy years. The promise is real and its timescale is rarely quoted with it.

31.t: I have drawn you with unfailing kindness. The verse immediately before the new covenant promise.
Written on hearts, with sins remembered no more. Jesus takes the phrase at the Last Supper, and Hebrews quotes the passage twice.

20.t: Jeremiah accuses God of overpowering him, then says the word is like fire in his bones and he cannot hold it in. Both are in the same paragraph.

32.t: With Babylon at the gates, Jeremiah buys land as a sign that houses and fields will be bought here again. Prophecy performed rather than spoken.

2.t: They have forsaken the spring of living water and dug their own cisterns, broken ones. Idolatry described as bad engineering.

7.t: Do not trust in deceptive words: the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD. Jesus quotes verse 11 when he clears the temple.

9.t: Boast in understanding and knowing the LORD. Paul quotes it twice to the Corinthians.

15.t: And I ate them; they were my joy and my heart's delight. Said by a man whose ministry brought him nothing but trouble.

23.t: Against Israel's leaders, followed by the promise of a righteous Branch from David. Ezekiel 34 makes the same move.

33.h: Call to me and I will answer
33.t: And tell you great and unsearchable things you do not know. Spoken while Jeremiah was under arrest.

38.t: Jeremiah sinks into the mud and is rescued by Ebed-Melech, a foreign official, using rags for padding under his arms. The detail is preserved because someone remembered it.

3.t: I am merciful, declares the LORD, I will not be angry for ever. Mercy offered in the middle of an indictment.

5.t: Jeremiah is told to search Jerusalem for a single honest man. He tries the poor, then the leaders, and finds none.

6.h: Peace, peace, where there is no peace
6.t: The charge against prophets and priests who dress the wound of the people as though it were not serious.

8.h: Is there no balm in Gilead
8.t: The question behind the spiritual. Jeremiah's grief is for a wound he cannot heal.

10.t: They cannot speak and must be carried because they cannot walk. A cucumber field is the image Jeremiah chooses.

12.h: Why does the way of the wicked prosper
12.t: Jeremiah's complaint, and God's answer is not comfort: if you have raced with men on foot and they have worn you out, how will you compete with horses.

18.t: The vessel is reshaped rather than discarded. Paul draws on the image in Romans 9.

25.t: The span Daniel is reading about in Daniel 9, and the basis for the return under Cyrus.

30.h: I will restore you to health
30.t: Because they called you an outcast, Zion for whom no one cares. The reason given is the contempt of others.

36.t: Jehoiakim cuts it up column by column and throws it in the fire. Jeremiah dictates it again, with more added.

39.t: The walls breached, the king blinded, the city burned. Ebed-Melech is spared because he trusted God.

45.t: Should you seek great things for yourself? Do not. A short, bracing word to the man who wrote the scroll.

52.t: Jehoiachin released from prison and given a seat at the king's table. Jeremiah ends, like Kings, on a very small hope.

4.t: Jeremiah describes the earth returning to formless and void — creation undone. The same Hebrew words as Genesis 1:2.

11.t: Jeremiah discovers a plot against him from his own home town. The image anticipates Isaiah 53.

13.t: Buried by a river until it rots. Israel was meant to cling to God like a belt and has become useless.

14.h: Do not pray for this people
14.t: God tells the prophet to stop interceding. One of the starkest verses in the book. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

16.t: Jeremiah is told not to take a wife or have children, as a sign of the coming catastrophe. His whole life becomes the message.

19.t: Smashed before the elders. What is shattered this way cannot be repaired.

21.h: The way of life and the way of death
21.t: Surrender to Babylon and live. The prophet's counsel sounded like treason.

22.h: Woe to him who builds by injustice
