22.t: A king building a palace with unpaid labour. To defend the poor, God says, is what it means to know me.

24.t: The exiles are the good figs; those left behind are the bad. The opposite of what everyone assumed.

26.t: He is saved because some elders remember that Micah prophesied the same thing a century earlier and was not killed.

27.t: Jeremiah wears an ox yoke as a sign to submit to Babylon.

28.t: A false prophet breaks Jeremiah's wooden yoke and promises release in two years. He dies within the year, as Jeremiah said.

34.t: Judah releases its slaves under covenant and then reclaims them. God calls it profaning his name.

35.t: A family who kept their ancestor's command for centuries, held up as a rebuke to Judah who would not keep God's.

37.h: Is there any word from the LORD
37.t: The king asks secretly. Jeremiah answers honestly, from prison, and then asks not to be sent back to the dungeon.

40.t: Offered a comfortable life in Babylon, he chooses to stay with the poor left in the ruined land.

41.t: The governor left in charge is murdered at dinner. The remnant falls apart.

42.t: The survivors ask Jeremiah to seek God's will, promise to obey, and when the answer is 'stay', they go to Egypt.

43.t: Jeremiah is carried off against his will by the people he warned. His ministry ends in exile in the land Israel was rescued from.

44.t: The refugees blame their disasters on stopping worship of a pagan goddess. Honest reasoning, entirely wrong.

46.t: The first of the oracles against the nations, which run to chapter 51.

47.h: Sword of the LORD, how long
47.t: A cry of pity in an oracle of judgement against the Philistines.

48.t: Like a flute. The prophet grieves even for enemies.

49.t: I will keep them alive. Mercy inside an oracle against Edom.

50.h: They will ask the way to Zion
50.t: Israel and Judah returning together, weeping, joining themselves to God in an everlasting covenant.

51.t: Tied to a stone and sunk: so Babylon will sink and not rise. The words of Jeremiah end here.

3.t: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases — placed at the exact centre of five poems about the destruction of Jerusalem, surrounded on both sides by devastation.

1.t: Look and see if there is any sorrow like mine. Read on Good Friday for obvious reasons.

5.t: The book ends without resolution: unless you have utterly rejected us. Scripture permits an unresolved ending.

2.t: The most unflinching chapter in Lamentations, describing God himself as the destroyer. Scripture does not flatten grief into comfort.

4.h: The gold has lost its lustre
4.t: Starving children and mothers in desperation. The horror of the siege recorded without softening. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: Wheels within wheels, and at the end the likeness of a throne and a figure on it. Ezekiel's careful hedging language — likeness, appearance — is the point.
Ezekiel piles up qualifiers because he is describing something he cannot describe. Then he falls face down.

34.t: God condemns Israel's leaders for feeding themselves and says he will search for his sheep himself. Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' is spoken against this background.
My servant David. Ezekiel's promise is the background to John 10.

36.t: I will show the holiness of my great name. The clearest statement in the prophets of why God restores.
Clean water, a heart of flesh for one of stone, and God's Spirit put within. The mechanics of the new covenant.

37.t: Can these bones live? Ezekiel's answer — O Lord GOD, you know — is the only honest one available to him.
The divided kingdom made one under one shepherd. The promise runs past anything the return from exile delivered.

18.t: Against the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes. Personal responsibility stated at length, ending with God taking no pleasure in the death of anyone.

33.t: If he does not warn, the blood is on him. It is the passage behind most of what the New Testament says about speaking up.

2.h: Whether they listen or fail to listen
2.t: Said four times. Faithfulness is defined by speaking rather than by results.

3.t: Sweet as honey in his mouth. John does the same thing in Revelation 10.

11.t: I will remove from them their heart of stone. Repeated more fully at 36:26.

16.t: Jerusalem as an abandoned infant, rescued, adorned and then unfaithful. It ends with God establishing his covenant anyway.

22.h: I looked for someone to stand in the gap
22.t: And found no one. One of the starkest verses on intercession in Scripture.

47.t: Ankle deep, knee deep, waist deep, then too deep to cross. Revelation 22 picks it up.

4.t: 390 days on one side and 40 on the other, cooking over dung. Prophecy performed with the prophet's own body.

8.h: What they do in the dark
8.t: Ezekiel is shown elders burning incense to idols in a hidden room, saying the LORD does not see us.

10.t: It moves from the threshold, then to the east gate, then away. The temple's destruction follows because God has already left.

12.t: Ezekiel packs his bags in daylight and leaves through a hole at dusk, as a sign of the coming exile.

14.t: Could save only themselves. Righteousness is not transferable, which is what makes the cross necessary.

20.h: For the sake of my name
20.t: Repeated through a long retelling of Israel's rebellion. God's reason for acting is his own character, not their merit.

24.t: Ezekiel is told not to mourn publicly, as a sign to the people. The cost of being a sign is real.

28.t: A lament using Eden imagery. Many read it as also describing a fall behind the human king; the text's primary subject is the king.

39.h: I will pour out my Spirit
39.t: On the house of Israel. The same promise as Joel, in a different register.

43.t: From the east, the way it left in chapter 10. The structure of the book turns on those two movements.

5.t: The hair divided into thirds: burned, struck, scattered. A drama of what is coming to Jerusalem.

6.t: Those who escape will remember me and loathe themselves. Repentance growing out of judgement.

7.t: Repeated like a drumbeat. Ezekiel's most concentrated judgement oracle.

9.h: A mark on those who grieve
9.t: Those who sigh over the city's sins are marked and spared. Revelation 7 echoes it.

13.t: False prophets cover over danger with 'peace'. God will bring the wall down on them.

15.t: Vine wood is good for nothing but burning, and even less after it has been burned.

17.t: God plants a cedar on a high mountain, and birds of every kind nest in it. Jesus' mustard seed parable draws on the image.

19.t: Judah's kings pictured as lions caught in nets.

21.h: Until he comes to whom it rightfully belongs
21.t: The crown removed from Zedekiah until a rightful king arrives. Read messianically from early on.

23.t: Two sisters representing Samaria and Jerusalem, in deliberately shocking sexual imagery about idolatry. It is meant to offend. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

25.t: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia judged for gloating over Judah's fall.

26.t: A bare rock for spreading nets. Conservative interpreters see it fulfilled in stages, with Alexander's destruction of the island city in 332 BC; others note Tyre was later rebuilt and read the oracle more generally. Either way, the great trading power of Ezekiel's day did not survive.

27.t: A lament picturing the city as a great merchant vessel that sinks. Revelation 18 borrows its cargo list.

29.t: The great monster in the Nile, claiming the river as his own creation.

30.t: Egypt's allies fall with her. Judah had repeatedly looked to Egypt for protection against Babylon, and Ezekiel's point is that the power they trusted instead of God cannot even save itself.

31.t: Assyria as a great tree brought down, a warning to Egypt.

32.t: Egypt joins the uncircumcised in the pit. A grim tour of fallen empires.

35.t: Edom judged for its ancient hostility and for rejoicing at Israel's ruin.

38.t: An end-times invasion defeated by God. Interpretations range from a specific future war to a symbolic picture of the final assault on God's people. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

40.t: Nine chapters of measurements. Readers divide on whether this describes a literal future temple, the church, or the new creation; Revelation 21 draws on it for the new Jerusalem. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

41.t: Measured precisely. Detail as an expression of holiness.

42.h: Separating the holy from the common
42.t: The purpose of the wall around the temple area.

44.t: The gate the glory entered is shut, because the LORD has come through it.

45.t: Rulers told to use honest weights and measures. The vision of worship includes economic justice.

46.t: Those who enter by the north go out by the south. No one leaves the way they came.

48.t: The last words of the book and the new name of the city. Everything Ezekiel saw leave returns.

2.t: Before he goes to the king, he blesses God for revealing the dream. Praise before delivery.
Four kingdoms and then a stone cut without hands that fills the earth. Identifications of the four are disputed; the conclusion is not.

3.t: The three refuse the image and say God can rescue them — but even if he does not, they will not bow. Faith that does not depend on the outcome.
Walking in the fire, unbound and unharmed. The king's description is left as he gave it.

6.t: On learning of the decree, Daniel changes nothing. The courage is in the ordinariness.

7.h: The Ancient of Days and the son of man
7.t: Two figures: one enthroned with hair white as wool, and one like a son of man given everlasting dominion. Jesus applies the second to himself at his trial; John describes him with details drawn from both.

9.t: He confesses sins he did not personally commit as though they were his own, which is worth noticing.

The most disputed prophecy in the Old Testament, with several serious interpretations. Note that verse 26 has the Anointed One cut off. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: Daniel negotiates rather than rebels, and is given favour. The whole book is about faithfulness inside a system rather than escape from it.

4.t: A pagan king's own testimony, in the first person, ending in praise. The most unexpected conversion account in the Old Testament.

5.t: Belshazzar uses the temple vessels at a feast. Weighed and found wanting, that same night.

12.t: One of the clearest Old Testament statements of bodily resurrection, to everlasting life or everlasting contempt.

10.h: Your words were heard from the first day
10.t: But the answer was delayed. A rare glimpse of something happening between prayer and answer.

8.t: Named in the text as Medo-Persia and Greece. The small horn is generally identified with Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC.

11.h: The kings of the north and south
11.t: The most detailed prophecy in Scripture, closely matching the history of the Ptolemies and Seleucids. Its precision is one reason critical scholars date the book late, and conservative scholars point to it as predictive prophecy. Worth talking through with a group leader, or an elder at your own church.

1.t: The prophet's life becomes the message. The children are given names that are sentences of judgement.

11.h: How can I give you up
11.t: God's internal conflict expressed as a parent's. My heart recoils within me, my compassion grows warm. Matthew quotes verse 1 of Jesus.

11.h: Out of Egypt I called my son
11.t: Quoted by Matthew of Jesus, reading Israel's history as fulfilled in him.

3.t: Hosea pays to redeem his own wife. The price is roughly that of a slave.

6.t: Quoted twice by Jesus in Matthew, both times to people who were technically correct and missing the point.

14.t: The book ends with an invitation and a promise to heal their waywardness and love them freely.

2.h: I will lead her into the wilderness
2.t: And speak tenderly to her. Judgement and wooing in the same sentence.

4.t: The charge is against priests who rejected knowledge, not against ignorant people.

5.h: Then I will return to my lair
5.t: Until they admit their guilt. God described as withdrawing deliberately.

7.h: A flat loaf not turned over
7.t: Burnt on one side and raw on the other. Hosea's image for half-hearted religion.

10.t: It is time to seek the LORD until he comes and showers righteousness on you.

12.t: Maintain love and justice, and wait for your God always.

13.h: Where, O death, is your victory
13.t: Paul takes this line into 1 Corinthians 15.

8.t: And reap the whirlwind. Consequences larger than the cause.

9.h: The prophet is considered a fool
9.t: Israel dismisses God's messengers as mad.

2.t: And not your garments. Return to the LORD, for he is gracious and compassionate — quoting Exodus 34.

2.h: I will pour out my Spirit
2.t: On all flesh — sons, daughters, old, young, male and female servants. Peter quotes it at Pentecost to explain what has happened.

1.t: Four waves, each finishing what the last left. Joel makes a natural disaster the occasion for national repentance.

3.t: A deliberate reversal of Isaiah 2, addressed to the nations rather than to Israel.

5.t: God rejects worship from people who trample the poor. Let justice roll on like a river — quoted by Martin Luther King Jr and often separated from its context, which is worship.

7.t: Amos insists he is a shepherd whom God took from tending the flock. Authority by calling rather than by office.

8.h: A famine of hearing the words
8.t: Not of bread or water. The judgement is silence.

1.h: For three sins, and for four
1.t: A circuit of the surrounding nations, each judged, before the pattern turns on Israel itself in 2:6. The audience would have been nodding along until then.

2.h: They sell the innocent for silver
2.t: And the needy for a pair of sandals. The specifics are what make Amos land.

3.t: Unless they have agreed to do so. A chain of rhetorical questions leading to: the Lord has spoken, who can but prophesy.

4.h: Yet you have not returned to me
4.t: Repeated five times after five disasters. Prepare to meet your God.

6.h: Woe to you who are complacent
6.t: Lying on beds inlaid with ivory and not grieved over the ruin of Joseph.

9.h: I will restore David's fallen shelter
9.t: James quotes this at the Jerusalem council as warrant for including the Gentiles.

1.t: Edom's sin is not attacking but watching and gloating while Jerusalem fell. As you have done, it will be done to you.
Jonah flees in the opposite direction from a mission he correctly suspects will succeed.

4.t: Jonah is angry precisely because God is gracious and relents. The book ends on God's question and no reply, which leaves the reader to supply one.

3.h: The word came a second time
3.t: Nineveh repents from the king down, and God relents. The shortest sermon in Scripture produces the largest response.

2.t: A psalm of thanksgiving, prayed before the rescue is complete. Jesus names the three days as the sign of his resurrection.

5.t: Small among the clans of Judah, and the origin of the ruler whose goings forth are from ancient days.

6.t: Act justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God. The summary of prophetic religion.

2.h: Those who plan iniquity on their beds
2.t: And carry it out at daylight because it is in their power. The prophets are consistently specific about land theft.

7.h: Who is a God like you
7.t: Pardoning sin, delighting to show mercy, hurling our iniquities into the depths of the sea. The name Micah means that first question.

1.t: Judgement on Samaria and Jerusalem, with the prophet going about barefoot and wailing.

3.t: Leaders who judge for a bribe and priests who teach for a price. Jeremiah 26 records this verse saving Jeremiah's life a century later.

4.h: Every man under his own vine
4.t: The nations stream to God's mountain, and each person lives in peace with no one to make them afraid.

1.h: Slow to anger and great in power
1.t: Nineveh, spared in Jonah, is now judged. Read alongside that book, the pair make a careful point about patience and its limits.

3.h: Woe to the city of blood
3.t: The fall of Nineveh described in detail. Read beside Jonah, the two books frame a century of patience and its end.

2.t: Vivid battle poetry: chariots in the streets, the palace collapsing.

1.t: The book opens with a complaint against God, which is where a good many honest believers start.
Habakkuk's second complaint is harder than his first: the remedy looks worse than the disease.

2.h: The righteous shall live by his faith
2.t: Quoted three times in the New Testament and central to the Reformation.

3.h: Though the fig tree does not bud
3.t: The most defiant statement of trust in Scripture. Nothing has improved; the poet has simply decided where to stand.

3.h: He will rejoice over you with singing
3.t: An unexpectedly tender verse at the end of a fierce book.

1.t: Described as wine left on its dregs, who say the LORD will do nothing either good or bad. Indifference judged as sharply as rebellion.

2.h: Seek the LORD, all you humble
2.t: Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of his anger. Hope offered to the humble inside a book of judgement.

1.t: The people say it is not time to build God's house while living in finished ones. Haggai's rebuke is two chapters long and entirely about priorities.

2.t: Greater than the former, though the builders could see it was smaller. Hebrews 12 quotes verse 6.

4.h: Not by might nor by power
4.t: Spoken to a governor facing a rebuilding project with no resources.

9.t: Riding on a donkey. All four Gospels connect it to the entry into Jerusalem.

12.h: They will look on me whom they have pierced
12.t: Quoted in John at the crucifixion and again in Revelation 1.

3.t: Joshua the high priest accused by Satan and clothed in clean garments instead. A picture of imputed righteousness.

8.h: Old men and children in the streets
8.t: The promised restoration described as ordinary life resuming. Streets safe enough for children to play in.

13.t: And the sheep will be scattered. Jesus quotes it on the night he is arrested.

1.t: And I will return to you. The first word of the book.

2.h: A wall of fire around her
2.t: Jerusalem will be too full for walls, and God himself will be its protection.

5.t: A curse going out against thieves and liars. Moral law enforced by God himself.

6.h: The Branch will be priest on his throne
6.t: King and priest united in one person. Hebrews develops the theme.

7.t: The answer to a question about fasting: show mercy and do not oppress the widow or the foreigner.

10.t: Jesus uses the phrase when he feeds the five thousand.

11.t: The shepherd's wages, thrown to the potter. Matthew connects it to Judas.

14.h: His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives
14.t: The mountain splits in two. Acts 1 has the ascension from the same mountain and the promise of return.

3.t: The forerunner who prepares the way — the verse Mark opens his Gospel by quoting.
The one place God invites his people to test him. Note the context: robbery, not investment.

4.t: The last words of the Old Testament look forward to a coming messenger, and four hundred years of silence follow.

1.t: Try offering it to your governor, God says. The animals were technically sacrifices and nobody was giving anything up.

2.t: In a passage about men discarding the wives of their youth. The context is faithlessness, and the language is strong.
